docs.title: Home
docs.text: Stenopos is a platform built so that an attack has nowhere to get through. It is three things that are designed together:

docs.title: Stenopos
docs.text: Ἀσφάλεια περὶ πλείστου · Security above all

docs.title: Stenopos OS
docs.text: A memory-safe, capability-based operating system: a small verified nucleus, every driver and service in its own compartment, and no root. It runs native apps, Debian packages and Windows programs.

docs.title: The Stenopos language
docs.text: The systems language the whole platform is written in. Memory safety, taint tracking, effect and capability types and constant-time secrets are checked by the compiler. Released today through Syntagma.

docs.title: Apps
docs.text: A shell, terminal, editor, browser, mail, calendar, app store and media player. Every one is an ordinary sandboxed package that you can remove or replace.

docs.title: What you can use today
docs.text:
The language and its toolchain are in release candidates:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh
tagma new hello && cd hello && tagma run

See Install, or the latest release. The OS and the apps are designed and not yet built; their pages explain the design. Status shows where every part stands.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text:
Please do not report security vulnerabilities in public issues.

Report them privately through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting: open the affected repository on GitHub, go to Security, and choose Report a vulnerability. Include steps to reproduce, the affected versions and, if you can, a proof of concept.

We will acknowledge your report, keep you informed, and credit you when the fix is released, unless you prefer to remain anonymous.

docs.title: Verifying what you download
docs.text:
Every release file is signed in CI with the Stenopos release key:

The installer checks the signature for you, against a copy of the key built into it.

docs.title: Apps
docs.text:
Stenopos OS comes with a suite of first-party apps. None of them is special: each is an ordinary, sandboxed .pano package that declares its capabilities like any other app, and each can be removed or replaced.

App What it is Hoplite (hop) The command shell Kopis The terminal Laconic The text and code editor Periplus The web browser and its memory-safe engine Keryx Mail and messaging Hemera The calendar Agora The app store Lyra The media player

Everyday utilities use plain names, so nobody has to learn a word to find them: Files, Settings, Updates, Passwords, Backup and Terminal.

docs.title: What every app gets
docs.text:
• Only what it declares. An app's manifest lists its capabilities, and you approve them, often at first use. Files come through the system file chooser, one at a time.
  • No silent network access, no reading other apps' windows, keystrokes or clipboard, and an unspoofable indicator whenever the camera, microphone or screen is in use.
  • Any language. Apps can be written in Stenopos or in C, C++, Rust, Go, Swift, Python, JavaScript or C#, with the same sandbox for all.

docs.title: Hoplite
docs.text:
Designed

Hoplite (hop) is the native command shell. It is structured: commands pass typed records and tables to each other, not text.

ls | where size > 10MB | sort-by modified

Output is a table for people, and to json, to csv or to text for programs.

docs.title: Capability-aware
docs.text:
Each command runs with only the capabilities its command line grants, plus those its manifest declares and you have approved. For example, compress ./photos -o out.zip can read ./photos and write out.zip, and nothing else.

  • Scripts declare what they need in a header. Running a downloaded script shows exactly what it will be able to touch, before it runs, and it cannot exceed that.
  • Arguments are passed as typed values and never re-split or re-parsed, so argument injection is impossible by construction.

docs.title: Scripting
docs.text: The scripting language is typed, with Stenopos-like syntax and safe quoting by construction. A script can grow into a compiled Stenopos program with few changes.

docs.title: Working with Linux tools
docs.text: bash, zsh, fish and the GNU tools run in Linux environments. The lx command opens one or runs a Linux command, and pipes cross between Hoplite and Linux commands, converting text to records where the format is known (JSON, CSV and common tools).

docs.title: System commands
docs.text: sten info (security tier and attestation), sten caps (grants), sten logs, sten update and sten env (Linux and Windows environments) all give structured output.

Not started

docs.title: What it will get from the platform
docs.text:
• Attachments are scanned on arrival by Phalanx Scan, in a sandbox with no capabilities.
  • Messages are parsed by memory-safe parsers, and everything from the network is tainted.
  • Passwords and tokens live in the system secrets store, and network access is limited to the mail servers you configure.

docs.title: Kopis
docs.text:
Designed

Kopis is the terminal: native, GPU-rendered through Eikon, and fast enough to meet the platform's latency and memory budgets.

docs.title: Escape sequences are hostile input
docs.text:
Terminals have a long history of escape-sequence injection bugs, where printing a malicious file makes the terminal act. Kopis parses every escape sequence as tainted input:

  • dangerous sequences, such as writing to the clipboard (OSC 52), title and report queries that echo input back, and hyperlinks, are filtered or need a capability;
  • inline images (sixel and kitty-style) are decoded in a sandbox.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Full Unicode, ligatures and true colour, with Hoplite as the default shell and Linux shells available in Linux environments.

docs.title: What it will get from the platform
docs.text:
• Files open through the system file chooser, so the editor can only touch the files you give it.
  • The Stenopos language server (stenopos lsp) for diagnostics, hover, go-to-definition and completion.
  • Text rendering and input through Morphe, with full Unicode, right-to-left scripts and sandboxed input methods.

docs.title: Lyra
docs.text:
Designed

Lyra is the media player, and the media framework every app uses to play and record audio and video.

docs.title: Built to open hostile files safely
docs.text:
• Files and streams are parsed by memory-safe Stenopos parsers in short-lived sandboxes with no capabilities, so a malicious video has nothing to attack and nothing to reach.
  • Hardware decoding is isolated, and decoded frames travel to the screen without copies.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
Files Format .mp4, .m4v, .m4a, .mov MP4 and QuickTime .mkv, .webm Matroska and WebM .ogg, .opus, .oga Ogg .ts, .m2ts MPEG transport stream .mp3, .flac, .aac, .wav, .aiff Audio files

Formats are recognised by their content, not their file name, and an unrecognised file is refused rather than guessed at.

docs.title: Codecs
docs.text:
Nothing in the base OS needs a patent licence:

Codec How it's decoded AV1, VP8, VP9, Opus, Vorbis, FLAC, MP3 Built in H.264, HEVC The device's hardware decoder where it has one; otherwise an opt-in codec package AAC The opt-in codec package, until its remaining patents lapse

The codec package is an ordinary signed package, offered the first time you open a file that needs it and installed only if you agree. Its decoders run in the same sandboxes. DRM is optional and confined.

docs.title: How it fits
docs.text: Lyra decodes. Aulos plays the sound on the right output, and Skene and Eikon show the video.

docs.title: Periplus
docs.text:
Designed

Stenopos OS offers three browsers, all first-class:

What it is Chromium A native port, pre-selected as the default Firefox A native port, offered with equal standing at setup Periplus A new, memory-safe browser engine written in Stenopos

Either of the first two can be removed, and both also run unmodified in a Linux environment from day one.

docs.title: Double sandboxing
docs.text: On Stenopos OS every site's renderer holds an empty capability set: no file, network, device or IPC access except channels to the browser's own processes. That is on top of the browser's own sandbox, so escaping it gains nothing.

docs.title: The Periplus engine
docs.text:
Periplus is compartmentalized per site. Every byte from the network is tainted, cookies and credentials are secret[T], and rendering, networking and TLS go through the OS's own Eikon, Dromos and Skytale.

It is delivered component by component, and each one hardens the whole OS as soon as it is ready:

Component Used across the OS for Image decoders (PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, GIF, SVG) All image decoding and thumbnails Font parsing and text shaping The UI toolkit and the terminal Media parsers The media framework HTML, CSS, URL and JSON parsers Help, rich text and manifests A JavaScript engine App scripting Layout and rendering Rich documents and the help viewer

Periplus becomes an optional browser, then the system web view's engine, then the default, each step only when measured results (Web Platform Tests and a top-sites corpus) say it is ready.

docs.title: Periplus WebView
docs.text: Apps that show web content use the system web view, a shared runtime patched once for every app. Its API doesn't depend on the engine: it starts on Chromium and can switch to Periplus with no change for apps.

docs.title: Devices
docs.text:
Stenopos OS is one operating system built into profiles for different devices. Each profile is the same verified system with a different set of parts compiled in. There is never a "lite" version with weaker security.

Profile For Idle memory target Desktops and laptops x86-64, ARM64 and RISC-V machines ≤ 400 MiB (1 GiB minimum RAM) Servers Cloud, bare metal, Kubernetes nodes ≤ 128 MiB Raspberry Pi Pi 3, 4 and 5, Zero 2 W ≤ 300 MiB as a desktop Embedded: Lochos Industrial, IoT, kiosks ≤ 32 MiB, in a ≤ 16 MiB image Phones and tablets: Trireme Phones with owner-enrolled boot keys (Phase 7)

docs.title: Security tiers
docs.text:
What the hardware can do decides how strong the isolation is, and Stenopos OS tells you which tier a machine runs at (on the boot screen, in Settings and with sten info):

Tier Needs Means 1: Full Compartment isolation, an IOMMU for every DMA-capable device, control-flow integrity in hardware, and a TPM Every guarantee in force 2: Strong Isolation and an IOMMU, but no hardware CFI or no TPM DMA isolation in force; less exploit hardening or no attestation 3: Mediated Isolation without an IOMMU (for example a Raspberry Pi 4) A verified DMA mediator checks device access; any driver it can't mediate is named as trusted

The tier is derived from the hardware at boot, never assumed, and recorded in the measured boot state so that a remote party can verify it. Policy can require a minimum tier: a password vault, for example, can insist on Tier 2.

All profiles are 64-bit and need an MMU with no-execute pages.

docs.title: Desktops and laptops
docs.text:
The full Stenopos Desktop on x86-64, ARM64 and RISC-V machines.

Budget Target Idle memory ≤ 400 MiB Minimum RAM 1 GiB (never more than 2 GiB) Boot to login, after firmware (NVMe) ≤ 3 s

Laptops get per-app energy accounting, power management for the CPU and devices, and battery, thermal and fan control through Krepis. Firmware updates for UEFI, SSDs, docks and peripherals are part of the system's own updates.

A PC with an IOMMU, a TPM and hardware control-flow integrity runs at Tier 1.

The desktop arrives in Phase 5 of the roadmap.

docs.title: Stenopos Lochos
docs.text:
Designed

Stenopos Lochos is the embedded and industrial profile: the same verified OS, compiled down to a minimal image. It is named for the smallest Spartan unit.

Budget Target Image size ≤ 16 MiB RAM, minimal headless device ≤ 32 MiB Interrupt-to-task latency (Pi-class hardware) ≤ 10 µs

docs.title: Hardware, one capability at a time
docs.text: GPIO, I²C, SPI, UART, PWM, ADC and DAC, CAN, 1-Wire and industrial Ethernet are capabilities per pin, channel, bus or device. An app controlling a motor gets that PWM channel and its GPIO pins, and nothing else.

docs.title: Built to run unattended
docs.text:
• Hard real time with guaranteed scheduling budgets, isolated from networking, logging and updates.
  • A hardware watchdog supervised by the nucleus, restartable compartments, and automatic rollback of failed updates.
  • A flash-wear-aware mode and safety on power loss.
  • Fleet updates: signed delta updates with staged rollout, resumable over poor links.
  • A signed lockdown policy: no shell, no SSH, a fixed set of apps, an allowlist of ports, debug interfaces off.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text: Every device has its own identity key, bound to hardware where possible, for attestation-based enrollment. There are no shared default passwords, ever.

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text:
MQTT over TLS 1.3, OPC UA, Modbus, CANopen and Matter/Thread, each a sandboxed component with scoped network and bus capabilities.

Microcontrollers without an MMU can't provide the isolation model, so they are out of scope; they talk to Lochos devices over these protocols.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
Stenopos OS supports the Raspberry Pi 3, 4 and 5 and the Zero 2 W, as a desktop, a server or an embedded device. Older 32-bit models (the Pi 1 and the original Zero) are not supported.

Budget Target Idle memory as a desktop ≤ 300 MiB Minimum RAM as a desktop 1 GiB Boot to login, after firmware (Pi 5) ≤ 6 s

docs.title: Security on a Pi
docs.text:
The Pi 4 has no IOMMU, so it runs at Tier 3: a verified DMA mediator checks every device access it can, and the tier report names any driver it can't. The Pi 5's IOMMU support is limited. Stenopos OS shows you exactly which tier your board runs at.

Pi firmware (the EEPROM) is updated through Krepis, like any other firmware. HAT overlays are applied declaratively and validated.

The Raspberry Pi 5 is one of the first two real-hardware targets, in Phase 3 of the roadmap.

docs.title: Servers
docs.text:
The server profile is headless and minimal, and it is the first public release of Stenopos OS (Phase 4 of the roadmap).

Budget Target Idle memory (SSH, network and storage) ≤ 128 MiB Minimum RAM 256 MiB Boot to ready, after firmware ≤ 2 s

docs.title: Managing a server
docs.text:
• Over SSH, which stays off until you configure it, with Hoplite and the sten commands.
  • Declarative configuration. The whole server state (packages, services, network, capability grants and policies) is one signed config file. It is applied atomically, reproducible across a fleet, and rolled back through snapshots.
  • Remote attestation. Clusters and orchestrators can refuse any node that isn't running a verified image at the required security tier.
  • The LTS channel gives five years or more of updates.

docs.title: Workloads
docs.text: Unmodified Docker and OCI images run in Oikos without a Linux kernel, Debian environments run apt-get as usual, and a Kubernetes-compatible node agent joins existing clusters. Stenopos OS also runs well as a guest on KVM, Hyper-V, VMware and Xen.

docs.title: Stenopos Trireme
docs.text:
Designed

Stenopos Trireme is the profile for phones and tablets, named for the fast Greek warship. It is designed now and built in Phase 7 of the roadmap.

docs.title: The modem is hostile
docs.text: The cellular modem is treated as a hostile network device: confined by the IOMMU to its own buffers, driven by its own compartment, and everything it sends is tainted. The OS keeps control of the modem's power, so airplane mode can cut it off entirely where the hardware allows.

docs.title: Phone features
docs.text:
• Calls (VoLTE, VoNR), SMS and MMS, RCS where possible, eSIM and dual SIM.
  • Emergency calls always work, even when locked and without a SIM.
  • The call log, messages and contacts are capabilities, granted per app.
  • One end-to-end encrypted push channel, compatible with UnifiedPush and self-hostable, so apps don't poll and nothing depends on Google or Apple.
  • Location, NFC and background sensor access are capabilities, with an indicator for location that apps cannot hide.
  • A phone shell built on the Tablet layout. Docking to a display switches to the desktop.

docs.title: Phones
docs.text: Trireme targets phones that let the owner enroll their own verified-boot keys: Google Pixel devices, Fairphone, and Linux phones such as the PinePhone and Librem 5.

docs.title: Language & Toolchain
docs.text:
Stenopos language: In progress Syntagma: In progress

Stenopos is the systems language the whole platform is written in. Its files are .sten. It reads like C, with braces, C-style declarations and no semicolons, and it makes security part of the type system:

  • Memory safety without a garbage collector. NOVA ownership tracking frees memory at compile-time-known points and rules out use-after-free and double frees. Threads share state only through chan, atomic and the locks; a data-race-freedom guarantee is planned, not yet checked.
  • Taint tracking. Untrusted input cannot reach a SQL query, a shell command or another sink until it passes a sanitizer.
  • Effects and capabilities. A function declares what it may do (@cap(File), @cap(Network)…), and the compiler holds it to that.
  • Constant-time secrets. secret[T] values cannot steer branches or memory access, so they cannot leak through timing.
  • Contracts, null safety and checked integer overflow, by default.
func main() -> int32 {
    str name = "Sparta"
    println("Hello, {name}!")
    return 0
}

docs.title: The toolchain: Syntagma
docs.text:
The language ships through Syntagma: the compiler (stenopos), the build tool (tagma), the standard library and the language server, released together under one version. See Syntagma, tagma and stenopos.

The compiler is self-hosting: it is written in Stenopos and compiles itself, and it builds for six Linux architectures.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• tagma, the build tool (ADR-0038). Syntagma now ships two commands: tagma for projects and stenopos, the compiler, for single files. tagma new, build, run, check, test, fmt, lint, doc and clean work on a directory with a Tagma.toml ([package] name, version and edition, plus local path [dependencies]). tagma calls the compiler's modules in-process and shares its version. The easter-egg commands moved from stenopos to tagma. See docs/TAGMA.md.
  • Editions. edition = "2026" in Tagma.toml names the language edition; the compiler refuses editions it does not know.
  • Release bundles. Each release ships syntagma-<version>-linux-<arch>.tar.gz (bin/tagma, bin/stenopos, lib/stenopos/ with the runtime and std) for all six architectures, plus standalone tagma-linux-<arch> binaries. The installer installs the bundle.
  • std.lock pins the std commit a release bundles and CI dogfoods, instead of choosing std by date.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• selfhost/ is now compiler/, and its modules are compiler.*.
  • The compiler finds its runtime and std beside its own binary (<prefix>/lib/stenopos/), so an install anywhere works without STENOPOS_HOME.
  • Inside a project, stenopos new and stenopos build/run/test without a file point to tagma.

  • The installer moved to public/install.sh (the one served from GitHub).

  • Generic structs as function return and parameter types. func make() -> Box[int32] and func f(Box[int32] b) now work (both were a clean error / silent int32). Generic struct templates are pre-registered before the signature pre-pass, so the concrete instance resolves in both collect_signatures and the body parse (parse_func/ parse_method); return Box { .. } resolves the generic literal against the declared return type. Forward references, methods, and multi-arg generics (Pair[int32, str]) all work, valgrind-clean. examples/generic_return.sten.

  • Conditional compilation: @cfg(...). A parse-time gate on top-level declarations, selected by build config — @cfg(target_arch == "x86_64"), @cfg(ptr_width == "64"), @cfg(profile == "release"), @cfg(feature == "debug"), with &&/||/! and ==/!=. Unlike a const-gated if (stripped only by the release optimizer, and still type-checked), @cfg is evaluated in the parser in BOTH passes, so an excluded declaration is never parsed, type-checked, or registered — enabling genuinely platform-specific code (e.g. x86_64-only inline asm invalid on aarch64), and two same-named @cfg variants coexist with no duplicate-definition error. Config comes from --target (arch/os/endian/ptr_width), --release (profile), and the new repeatable --feature NAME / --define NAME. examples/cfg_select.sten.
  • Top-level const globals. const int32 W = 10 (and int64/uint32/ float64/bool/str) at file scope declares a named, immutable, compile-time literal constant visible to every function in the file. It is substituted in place at each use — no storage, no indirection — so a global const name is never an assignable slot. Initializers must be a literal of the declared type; a computed expression or a type mismatch is a clean error. A local may shadow a global const. examples/const_globals.sten.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Block-local variables are now correctly scoped. A name declared inside a block ({ } of an if/while/for/do/try/with/match/unsafe) was leaking out — a nested int32 x = 2 overwrote an outer x, and the inner binding stayed visible after the block. Now a nested declaration is local to its block: shadowing is restored on block exit, sibling blocks reuse names freely, and using a block-local after its block is undefined variable. Implemented WITHOUT popping names (a block-horizon stack + a sparse dead-set), so slots stay monotonic and the const/color/codegen paths are unchanged. examples/scoping.sten. (Follow-up: reject same-scope redeclaration.)
  • Passing a fixed array directly to a slice parameter is now a clean error. f(a) where a: int32[3] and f takes int32[] used to be accepted but read garbage (.len() returned 1) and segfaulted on iteration — a fixed array is not a {len,ptr} slice view. Slice it first: f(a[0..<3]). examples/compile-fail/array_as_slice.sten.
  • Returning a generic struct type is now a clean error, not a silent mis-compile. func make() -> Box[int32] previously either failed with a confusing parse error or (as a forward reference) silently recorded int32 and returned garbage, because the signature pre-pass runs before generic structs are registered. It now reports that the case isn't supported yet (return a concrete struct or the inner value). Full support is a generics follow-up. examples/compile-fail/generic_return_type.sten.
  • do { ... } while (cond) is now implemented. It previously parsed but emitted NOTHING — the body and everything after it in the function silently vanished. It now compiles to a proper bottom-checked loop (the body runs at least once, the condition is tested at the bottom; break/continue work), and a do not followed by while (cond) is a clean parse error. examples/do_while.sten.
  • Reassigning a nullable struct/str field no longer emits ill-typed IR. t.left = insert(t.left, v) where left: Tree? stored a raw pointer into the {i1, ptr} nullable slot (rejected by llc), which blocked linked lists and trees built by field mutation. The assignment now widens a bare T -> T? (and drops the replaced inner, null-safe), so building and overwriting are both valgrind-clean. examples/bst_mutate.sten.
  • A local const declaration no longer silently drops its initializer. const int32 x = 42 previously parsed but left x empty (the const modifier was never consumed, so the declaration mis-parsed); const is now a recognized declaration modifier and the value is kept.
  • const immutability is now enforced. Reassigning a const — local (const int32 x = 1 then x = 2) or global (W = 5 on a top-level const, which used to crash with an out-of-bounds write) — is a clean compile error. Covers = and the compound forms. examples/compile-fail/const_reassign.sten.
  • A struct literal naming an unknown field is now rejected. Point { x: 1, zz: 9 } where zz is not a field previously mapped the stray value to field 0 (silently overwriting x); it now reports "struct 'Point' has no field 'zz'" (the field-index lookup returned 0 on a miss). examples/compile-fail/struct_lit_unknown_field.sten.
  • Calling an rwlock-only method on a mutex/spinlock (or vice versa) is now a clean error. m.read_lock() on a mutex[T] previously type-checked and emitted a nonsensical call; the parser now validates each lock method against its lock kind (lock/unlock for mutex/spinlock, read_lock/write_lock for rwlock, acquire/release for semaphore) and reports e.g. "mutex has no method read_lock". examples/compile-fail/lock_bad_method.sten.
  • sort() on a List whose element has no natural order is now a clean error. .sort() on a List[struct] (or a float/bool/enum list) previously fell through to the 4-byte sort_i32 path and read each element at the wrong width — a silent mis-compile. It now reports "sort needs an int32, int64, or str element type". examples/compile-fail/list_sort_struct.sten.

docs.title: Which file do I need?
docs.text:
File What it is syntagma-<version>-linux-<arch>.tar.gz Everything: tagma, stenopos, the runtime and the standard library. This is what the installer installs tagma-linux-<arch>, stenopos-linux-<arch> The two commands on their own stenopos-std.tar.gz, stenopos_runtime.c The standard library and the runtime on their own stenopos-bootstrap-seed-x86_64 The seed compiler the self-hosted bootstrap starts from install.sh The installer SHA256SUMS, *.asc Checksums and signatures

Earlier releases: all Syntagma releases.

docs.title: As a project
docs.text:
tagma new hello
cd hello
tagma run

tagma new creates:

hello/
├── Tagma.toml
├── .gitignore
└── src/
    └── main.sten

src/main.sten is the program:

func main() -> void {
    println("Hello from hello!")
}

and tagma run builds it to target/draft/hello and runs it.

docs.title: As a single file
docs.text:
The compiler builds one file with no project:

func main() -> int32 {
    println("Hello, world!")
    return 0
}

stenopos run hello.sten

docs.title: What each line means
docs.text:
• func main() -> int32 { is the entry point. It returns the exit code; -> void means "exit with 0".
  • println(...) prints a line. It is built in, so there is nothing to import, and {...} inside a string interpolates a value.
  • return 0: exit code 0 means success.
  • Braces mark blocks; a new line ends a statement.

docs.title: String interpolation
docs.text:
func main() -> int32 {
    str name = "Stenopos"
    println("Hello, {name}!")
    return 0
}

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Projects with tagma: dependencies, tests and builds.
  • The Language Guide: variables, types and control flow.

docs.title: The installer (recommended)
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

The installer finds your CPU architecture, downloads the newest Syntagma release (pre-releases included), checks its signature against the Stenopos release key built into the installer, checks the SHA-256 checksum, and installs:

What Where tagma, the build tool /usr/local/bin stenopos, the compiler /usr/local/bin The runtime and the standard library /usr/local/lib/stenopos

Both commands find the runtime and library beside themselves, so nothing needs configuring.

Setting Effect STENOPOS_VERSION=v1.0.0-rc.5 Install a specific release STENOPOS_INSTALL=$HOME/.local/bin Install somewhere else (the library goes in the sibling lib/stenopos) STENOPOS_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE=1 Refuse to install if gpg is missing and the signature can't be checked

Stenopos needs llc (LLVM 14 or newer) and cc (a C compiler) when it compiles:

sudo apt-get install -y llvm clang     # Debian and Ubuntu
brew install llvm                      # macOS

docs.title: Supported systems
docs.text: Linux on six architectures: x86_64, aarch64, ppc64le, riscv64, armv7 and s390x, including 32-bit (armv7) and big-endian (s390x). Any of them can cross-compile for the others.

docs.title: By hand
docs.text:
Each release has a bundle per architecture, syntagma-<version>-linux-<arch>.tar.gz, containing bin/tagma, bin/stenopos and lib/stenopos/. Unpack it anywhere and put its bin/ on your PATH:

tar -xzf syntagma-1.0.0-rc.5-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
export PATH="$PWD/syntagma-1.0.0-rc.5-linux-x86_64/bin:$PATH"

See Downloads for the files and how to verify them.

docs.title: Check the install
docs.text:
tagma version
stenopos version

docs.title: How the compiler is built
docs.text: The compiler is written in Stenopos and builds itself. Each release also publishes the seed compiler that its bootstrap starts from (stenopos-bootstrap-seed-x86_64), and every build checks that the compiler, rebuilt by itself, produces identical output. The source is not published yet.

docs.title: If / else
docs.text:
Parentheses around the condition are required:

if (x > 0) {
    println("positive")
} else if (x < 0) {
    println("negative")
} else {
    println("zero")
}

docs.title: Ternary
docs.text:
Coming in 1.0

Not implemented yet.

int32 abs_x = if (x >= 0) x else -x

docs.title: For loops
docs.text:
// inclusive range (0 through 9)
for (i in 0..9) {
    println("{i}")
}

// exclusive range (0 through 9, not 10)
for (i in 0..<10) {
    println("{i}")
}

docs.title: While
docs.text:
while (counter < 100) {
    counter = counter + 1
}

docs.title: Do-while
docs.text:
do {
    counter = counter + 1
} while (counter < 100)

docs.title: Repeat
docs.text:
Coming in 1.0

Not implemented yet.

repeat (5) {
    println("hello")
}

docs.title: Match
docs.text:
A case uses the colon form: the statements after the : run until the next case or the closing }. Patterns are literals, enum variants, or _ for the catch-all.

match (status) {
    case 200: println("OK")
    case 404: println("Not found")
    case _: println("Unknown: {status}")
}

Coming in 1.0: range patterns

case 500..599: (inclusive) and case 500..<600: (exclusive).

A case can run several statements — they all belong to the case until the next case:

match (status) {
    case 200:
        log("serving")
        println("OK")
    case _:
        println("Unknown: {status}")
}

Enum variants match by their qualified name, and payload fields bind as names. A variant with a payload lists its field types:

enum Shape : int32 {
    Circle(float64)
    Rect(float64, float64)
    Empty
}

match (shape) {
    case Shape.Circle(r): return 3.14159 * r * r
    case Shape.Rect(w, h): return w * h
    case Shape.Empty: return 0.0
}

docs.title: Break and continue
docs.text:
for (i in 0..<100) {
    if (i == 50) {
        break
    }
    if (i % 2 == 0) {
        continue
    }
    println("{i}")
}

docs.title: Try / catch / finally
docs.text:
throw raises an error with a message; catch receives it:

func parse_port(str s) -> int32 {
    if (s.len() == 0) {
        throw("empty port")
    }
    return 8080
}

func main() -> int32 {
    try {
        int32 p = parse_port("")
        println("{p}")
    } catch (Error e) {
        println("error: {e}")
    } finally {
        println("done")
    }
    return 0
}

The finally block always runs, whether or not an error occurred. Library functions report failures the same way: std.base64's base64_decode throws on malformed input, for example.

Coming in 1.0

Typed errors (catch (IOError e)), several catch clauses tried in order, and an error value with fields such as e.message.

docs.title: With (scoped cleanup)
docs.text:
with holds a resource for a block and releases it when the block ends, on every path. Locks use it today:

mutex[int32] m = mutex(0)
with (g = m.guard()) {
    g.set(g.get() + 1)
}
// the lock is released here

Coming in 1.0

Files: with (File f = open("log.txt")) { f.write("entry\n") }.

docs.title: Defer
docs.text:
defer schedules an expression to run when its enclosing block exits — by any path: falling off the end, an early return, a break/continue, or a throw. Deferred expressions run last-in-first-out, and before the block's locals are freed, so cleanup can still use them.

func process() -> void {
    println("open")
    defer println("close")   // runs no matter how process() exits
    println("work")
    // ... "close" prints here automatically ...
}

defer is block-scoped: a defer inside a loop body fires at the end of each iteration, not all at once when the function returns.

for (i in 0..2) {
    defer println("close {i}")
    println("open {i}")
}
// open 0 / close 0 / open 1 / close 1 / open 2 / close 2

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
@requires and @ensures attach a precondition and a postcondition to a function. Both are boolean expressions checked at run time; @ensures also sees the returned value as result. A violated contract reports which one failed and stops the program — a broken assumption halts at the boundary that stated it, instead of corrupting whatever comes next.

@requires(n >= 0)
@ensures(result >= 1)
func factorial(int32 n) -> int32 {
    if (n <= 1) {
        return 1
    }
    return n * factorial(n - 1)
}

Several @requires may be stacked; each is checked on entry.

docs.title: Nested error handling
docs.text:
try blocks nest; an error is caught by the innermost catch around it:

try {
    try {
        throw("inner")
    } catch (Error e) {
        println("caught {e}")
        throw("outer")
    }
} catch (Error e) {
    println("then caught {e}")
}

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text:
func add(int32 a, int32 b) -> int32 {
    return a + b
}

func greet(str name) -> void {     // `-> void` is required
    println("Hello, {name}!")
}

Return values are must-use: calling add(1, 2) and ignoring the result is a compile error. Use it, assign it, discard add(1, 2) to drop it on purpose, or mark the function @ignore_discard.

docs.title: Generic functions
docs.text:
func identity[T](T val) -> T {
    return val
}

int32 n = identity(7)
str s = identity("hi")

docs.title: Lambdas
docs.text:
A lambda's parameters and return type are written out. Its type is fn(parameter types)->return type:

fn(int32)->int32 square = |int32 n| -> int32 {
    return n * n
}

fn()->void hello = || -> void {
    println("hello")
}

func apply(fn(int32)->int32 f, int32 x) -> int32 {
    return f(x)
}

A lambda can use variables from where it's defined (captures them).

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Methods are written inside a struct or class, and reach the value as this:

struct Point {
    float64 x
    float64 y

    pub func norm2() -> float64 {
        return this.x * this.x + this.y * this.y
    }
}

docs.title: Coming in 1.0
docs.text:
Not implemented yet

These are part of the 1.0 language and are being built.

// Default parameters
func connect(str host = "localhost", int32 port = 8080) -> bool {
    return true
}

// Named arguments
connect(port: 443, host: "example.com")

// Multiple return values via tuples
func divmod(int32 a, int32 b) -> (int32, int32) {
    return (a / b, a % b)
}
(int32 q, int32 r) = divmod(17, 5)

// Methods declared outside the type
func (Point p).distance() -> float64 {
    return sqrt(p.x * p.x + p.y * p.y)
}

// Functions evaluated at compile time
const func factorial(int32 n) -> int32 {
    if (n <= 1) {
        return 1
    }
    return n * factorial(n - 1)
}
const int32 F10 = factorial(10)

docs.title: Memory Safety
docs.text: Stenopos manages memory with NOVA: no garbage collector and no manual free. The compiler inserts every allocation's release at the point the value's owner goes away.

docs.title: Freed at the end of scope
docs.text:
func process() -> void {
    str data = "a string on the heap"
    println(data)
    // data is freed here, automatically
}

Strings, lists and maps free their memory when their owner leaves scope, on every path out: falling off the end, return, break, continue or a throw. There is no use-after-free, no double free and no leak, and the CI checks the whole test corpus under valgrind.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
Every value has exactly one owner.

Today, handing a value to a new owner copies it: after str b = a, a and b are independent, and changing one never affects the other. This is always safe; the compiler already avoids the copy when a is not used again.

Coming in 1.0: moves (ADR-0040)

Values that own heap memory (str, List, HashMap, and structs that contain them) will move instead: after str b = a, a can no longer be used, and the compiler reports it if you try. Copying becomes explicit with .clone(). Numbers, bool and structs of plain data still copy implicitly. A parameter borrows (the function reads the value and the caller keeps it) unless the function keeps it, by storing or returning it: then the parameter consumes the value, and the compiler infers which without any annotation.

str a = "hello"
str b = a          // a moves into b
println(a)         // error: use of moved value `a`
str c = b.clone()  // an explicit, independent copy

Moves make transfers free (no hidden copies), let messages and channels hand data over without copying, and let capabilities be values that can't be duplicated.

docs.title: Raw pointers
docs.text:
For talking to C, raw pointers exist, confined to unsafe blocks:

func main() -> void {
    int32 x = 41
    unsafe {
        ptr[int32] p = &x
        *p = *p + 1
    }
    println("{x}")     // 42
}

Dereferencing a pointer and calling an extern C function require unsafe.

Coming in 1.0 (ADR-0041)

Every use of a raw pointer will require unsafe, including taking an address with &x and holding a ptr[T], so the unsafe blocks are the complete list of places to audit.

docs.title: Calling C
docs.text:
extern "C" {
    func abs(int32 n) -> int32
    func labs(int64 n) -> int64
}

func main() -> void {
    unsafe {
        println("{abs(0 - 7)} {labs(0 - 9)}")
    }
}

Limits today

An extern function's parameters and result must all be int32, or all int64. Pointers, strings, structs and mixed types are coming (PLAN M8).

docs.title: No null dereferences
docs.text: Nullable values (T?) must be checked before use; the compiler narrows the type after the check (see Variables and Types). Raw pointers will follow the same rule as ptr[T]?.

docs.title: Declaring a module
docs.text: module math.vector

docs.title: Visibility: pub vs. private
docs.text:
Declarations are private to their module by default. A function, struct, enum, trait, or type alias is only visible to code in the same module unless you mark it pub. Reaching for a private name from another module is a compile error:

module math.internal

pub func cube(int32 n) -> int32 {   // public API — callable anywhere
    return n * square(n)
}

func square(int32 n) -> int32 {     // private — only this module may use it
    return n * n
}

module app.main

import math.internal.{cube}

func main() -> void {
    println("{cube(3)}")            // ok — cube is pub
    // println("{square(3)}")       // compile error: square is private to math.internal
}

This keeps a module's surface area deliberate: callers depend only on what you chose to expose, and you can refactor everything else freely.

docs.title: Importing
docs.text:
Name what you use from a module in braces:

import math.vector.{Vec3, Vec4}
import std.string.{split, trim}

The compiler finds a module by its module line, in the project's own files, its dependencies (see tagma) and the standard library.

Coming in 1.0

import math.vector.Vec3      // one name, without braces
import math.vector.*         // every public name
import self.utils            // relative to this module
import super.shared          // relative to the parent module
pub import math.vector.Vec3  // re-export to this module's importers

docs.title: Example layout
docs.text:
src/
  main.sten          module app
  math/
    vector.sten      module math.vector
    matrix.sten      module math.matrix

A module may live in any file; its module line names it. Keeping the path and the module name in step makes a project easy to navigate.

docs.title: Language Guide Overview
docs.text: Stenopos is a statically typed systems language with C-style brace syntax and no semicolons. This guide walks through the core language features.

docs.title: Design goals
docs.text:
• Readable — curly-brace blocks, no semicolons
  • Safe by default — memory safety, taint tracking, effect types built into the type system
  • C-compatible — call C libraries directly (extern "C")
  • One toolchain — tagma builds, runs, tests, formats and lints projects; stenopos, the compiler, does the same for single files

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Variables and Types
  • Functions
  • Control Flow
  • Structs and Classes
  • Memory Safety
  • Error Handling
  • Modules

docs.title: Structs
docs.text:
Plain data containers:

struct Point {
    float64 x
    float64 y
}

Point p = Point { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 }
println("{p.x}, {p.y}")

Structs and classes can have methods, which reach the value as this:

struct Point {
    float64 x
    float64 y

    pub func norm2() -> float64 {
        return this.x * this.x + this.y * this.y
    }
}

docs.title: Generic structs
docs.text:
struct Pair[A, B] {
    A first
    B second
}

Pair[int32, str] p = Pair { first: 7, second: "seven" }

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
Classes add inheritance. Like structs, they are values: a class instance lives where its variable lives, with no hidden heap allocation and no garbage collector.

class Animal {
    pub str name

    virtual func speak() -> void {
        println("...")
    }
}

class Dog : Animal {
    override func speak() -> void {
        println("Woof! I'm {this.name}")
    }
}

Use parent to call the parent class method:

class Puppy : Dog {
    override func speak() -> void {
        parent.speak()
        println("*wags tail*")
    }
}

A derived value is never silently converted to its base type (that would drop its fields). For polymorphism, use dyn:

class Shape {
    virtual func name() -> str {
        return "shape"
    }
}

class Square : Shape {
    override func name() -> str {
        return "square"
    }
}

Square sq = Square {}
dyn Shape s = sq
println(s.name())        // square

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text:
Fields and methods are private by default; pub makes them visible outside their module.

class BankAccount {
    float64 balance                 // private

    pub func deposit(float64 amount) -> void {
        this.balance += amount
    }

    pub func get_balance() -> float64 {
        return this.balance
    }
}

docs.title: Traits
docs.text:
trait Describe {
    func describe() -> str
}

impl Describe for Point {
    func describe() -> str {
        return "({this.x}, {this.y})"
    }
}

A trait object, dyn Describe, holds any value whose type implements the trait:

dyn Describe d = Point { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 }
println(d.describe())

Traits can be implemented for types you didn't write, including primitives.

docs.title: Coming in 1.0
docs.text:
Not implemented yet

  • protected members, visible to the class and its subclasses.
  • Referring to a field inside a method without this..
  • Abstract methods: abstract func area() -> float64 in a class, which every subclass must override.
  • clone(), a deep copy (part of ownership and moves).
  • Calling a void method through dyn, methods with arguments through dyn, and passing a concrete value where a dyn parameter is expected.

docs.title: Statements & Line Breaks
docs.text:
Stenopos uses newline as the statement terminator — like Go, and unlike C. There are no semicolons. Write one statement per line:

int32 x = 42
int32 y = x + 1
println("{y}")

Blank lines are ignored, so use them freely to group code. Indentation is not significant (blocks are delimited by braces), but 4-space indentation is the convention.

docs.title: Breaking a long line
docs.text: A newline ends a statement only when the line so far could be a complete statement. In the two situations below the newline is treated as a space and the statement continues — the same rule Go uses. There is no line-continuation character (a \ is not special here).

docs.title: 1. After an operator that needs a right-hand side
docs.text:
A line that ends on an operator which cannot finish a statement — a binary, comparison, logical, bitwise, or assignment operator, ??, a trailing ., or -> — continues onto the next line:

int32 total = first_value +
              second_value +
              third_value

if (ready &&
    count > 0) {
    // ...
}

Method-call chains break the same way, on a trailing .:

str result = name.trim().
    to_upper()

(The . must end the upper line. A line that ends on a complete value — e.g. name.trim() — terminates, so a .method() cannot start the next line.)

docs.title: 2. Inside brackets ( … ) and [ … ]
docs.text:
Newlines between a matching (/) or [/] are ignored, so call arguments, function parameters, array/list literals, and parenthesized expressions may span lines:

int32 s = add(
    add(1, 2),
    add(3, 4))

func distance(float64 x,
              float64 y) -> float64 {
    return x * x + y * y
}

int32[3] triple = [10,
                   20,
                   30]

No trailing comma

Close the list right after the last element (3) above, not 3,)). A trailing comma before the closing bracket is a syntax error.

docs.title: String interpolation
docs.text:
Inside an interpolated string, "{ ... }" holds an expression that is evaluated and formatted in place. The whole string literal stays on a single source line:

str name = "Stenopos"
println("Hello, {name}! 1 + 1 = {1 + 1}")

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: You want to… Do this End a statement Start a new line (no ;) Continue a long expression End the line on an operator (+, &&, =, a trailing ., …) — it carries to the next line Spread call args / parameters / a list literal Break after a comma inside (…) or […] — no trailing comma Group code visually Use blank lines (ignored)

docs.title: Declarations
docs.text:
Variables are declared with the type before the name — C style, not Rust style.

int32 x = 42
int64 big = 1000000
float64 pi = 3.14159
str greeting = "hello"
bool flag = true

docs.title: Mutable by default
docs.text:
All variables are mutable. Use const to make something immutable:

const int32 MAX = 100
int32 counter = 0
counter = counter + 1   // ok
// MAX = 200            // compile error

docs.title: Numeric types
docs.text:
Type Size Range int32 32-bit signed -2^31 to 2^31-1 int64 64-bit signed -2^63 to 2^63-1 uint32 32-bit unsigned 0 to 2^32-1 uint64 64-bit unsigned 0 to 2^64-1 float64 64-bit float IEEE 754

int8, int16, uint8, uint16 and float32 are reserved for later; using one today is a compile error.

Unsigned types are unsigned everywhere: comparison, /, % and >> treat the top bit as part of the value. An unsigned value can't be negated, and going below zero is an overflow.

Integer literals can be written in decimal, hex (0x) or binary (0b), and hex and binary may use _ to group digits (_ in decimal literals is coming in 1.0). A literal takes the type of the integer it is used with:

func main() -> int32 {
    uint64 mask = 0xffff_ffff_0000_0000
    uint32 flags = 0b1010
    println("{mask >> 32} {flags % 4}")
    return 0
}

No implicit numeric conversions. Use cast[T]() to convert explicitly:

int32 x = 42
int64 y = cast[int64](x)

docs.title: Integer overflow is checked
docs.text:
Arithmetic that overflows its type is a bug — and a frequent source of security holes, where a wrapped size calculation leads to an undersized buffer. Stenopos does not let it happen silently. Every +, -, and * on an integer (signed or unsigned) is checked; if the result does not fit the type, the program stops with a diagnostic instead of wrapping to a wrong value:

int32 x = 2147483647    // int32 max
int32 y = x + 1         // aborts: "integer overflow: add of two int32 values"

This applies to compound assignments (+=, -=, *=) too. In-range arithmetic is unaffected, and the check is cheap — it compiles to an add plus a jump-on-overflow, not a software division.

docs.title: Opting out: wrapping_*
docs.text:
Some algorithms want modular arithmetic — hashes, checksums, PRNGs, ring-buffer indices. For those, ask for wrapping explicitly with wrapping_add, wrapping_sub, and wrapping_mul:

// FNV-1a hash — defined in terms of wrapping arithmetic, so it says so.
func fnv1a(str s) -> uint32 {
    uint32 hash = 2166136261
    int64 i = 0
    while (i < s.len()) {
        hash = wrapping_mul(hash, 16777619)
        hash = wrapping_add(hash, cast[uint32](s.byte_at(i)))
        i += 1
    }
    return hash
}

The default is safe; wrapping is opt-in and visible at the call site.

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
int64[5] numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
int64 first = numbers[0]

Every index is bounds-checked: an index out of range stops the program instead of reading or writing memory it shouldn't. The C-style declaration int64 numbers[5] = ... is coming in 1.0.

docs.title: Nullable types
docs.text:
Any type T has a nullable form T? that holds either a value or null. The compiler will not let you use a T? as a T until you have ruled out null.

int32? maybe = null
str? name = "Stenopos"

Compare against null with == / !=. After a check, the value is narrowed to the non-nullable type for the rest of that scope:

func classify(int32? n) -> str {
    if (n == null) {
        return "none"
    }
    // n is narrowed to plain int32 here
    return "value: {n}"
}

Three operators work on nullables:

int32? missing = null
int32 x = missing ?? 0          // ?? — fallback when the left side is null
int32? forced = 7
int32 y = forced!!              // !! — assert non-null (aborts at runtime if null)
int64 len = name?.len() ?? 0    // ?. — safe access, yields a nullable

There is no null-pointer dereference: raw pointers are nullable with the same ptr[T]? syntax and must be checked before use inside unsafe.

docs.text:

docs.title: Memory (NOVA)
docs.text:
Automatic, leak-free memory with no garbage collector; heap buffers are freed when their owner leaves scope. Today a transfer copies; (1.0) owning values move and .clone() copies (Memory Safety).

unsafe {
    ptr[int32] p = &x
    int32 val = *p
}

docs.title: Annotations
docs.text:
Annotation Purpose @cap(File\|Process\|Network\|Memory\|System) Declare a capability; callers must declare it too @pure / @io / @net Effects @tainted / @sanitizer / @sink Taint tracking @requires(cond) / @ensures(cond) Contracts (result is the return value); several are joined with && @sensitive Wipe the value's memory when it is freed @ignore_discard Callers may drop the return value @deprecated("msg") Callers get a warning @inline / @hot / @cold Inlining and code-placement hints @no_return The function never returns (return is an error; reaching the end aborts) @section("name") Place the function in a linker section @module_init / @module_exit A module's entry and exit points (.init.text / .exit.text) @repr("C") Lay a struct out exactly as C does (every field must have a C equivalent) @test A test function @cfg(...) Conditional compilation (target_arch, ptr_width, profile, feature); comes first

Annotations work the same on methods as on functions. An unknown or misplaced annotation is a compile error. (1.0): @packed, @aligned(N) and @opaque are rejected until C-compatible layouts land; annotations on struct fields and the call-site annotations on generic functions are not supported yet.

docs.title: Cross-compilation
docs.text:
Stenopos can build a binary for a different CPU than the one you are compiling on, in one command:

stenopos build --target aarch64 -o app-arm64 main.sten

That produces an ARM64 Linux executable from, say, an x86-64 laptop. No separate steps, no hand-run llc.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: The compiler emits target-neutral LLVM IR — it does not bake in a CPU or a memory layout. So the same compiled program can be lowered for any supported CPU; --target just tells the backend which one, and picks the matching cross C compiler to link with.

docs.title: Supported targets
docs.text:
--target Architecture Notes x86_64 64-bit Intel/AMD the host default aarch64 (alias arm64) 64-bit ARM phones, Raspberry Pi 4/5, Apple-class ppc64le 64-bit PowerPC (little-endian) riscv64 64-bit RISC-V hard-float armv7 (alias arm) 32-bit ARM (hard-float) Raspberry Pi 2/3, many embedded boards s390x 64-bit IBM Z (big-endian) i686 (alias x86) 32-bit Intel/AMD older / smaller x86 devices mipsel 32-bit MIPS (little-endian) routers, embedded mips64el 64-bit MIPS (little-endian) powerpc (alias ppc) 32-bit PowerPC (big-endian) routers, older Macs, embedded mips 32-bit MIPS (big-endian) routers, embedded

You can pass either the short name (aarch64) or the full triple (aarch64-linux-gnu).

All eleven run correct programs — every byte order and word size (32- and 64-bit, little- and big-endian) — checked on every change, so a target on this list will not silently break.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
--target shells out to the matching cross toolchain, so it must be installed:

Target Package (Debian/Ubuntu) aarch64 gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu ppc64le gcc-powerpc64le-linux-gnu riscv64 gcc-riscv64-linux-gnu armv7 gcc-arm-linux-gnueabihf s390x gcc-s390x-linux-gnu i686 gcc-i686-linux-gnu mipsel gcc-mipsel-linux-gnu mips64el gcc-mips64el-linux-gnuabi64 powerpc gcc-powerpc-linux-gnu mips gcc-mips-linux-gnu

If the toolchain is missing, the compiler says exactly which package to install.

docs.title: Running the result
docs.text:
A cross-built binary runs on the real target device. To try it on your build machine, use an emulator:

stenopos build --target aarch64 -o app-arm64 main.sten
qemu-aarch64-static -L /usr/aarch64-linux-gnu ./app-arm64

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• --target is a build-only option — run, check, and emit-* ignore it (you cannot execute a foreign-CPU binary directly on the host).
  • Every cross build is Linux/ELF and keeps the same security hardening as a native build (PIE, full RELRO, non-executable stack, stack canaries).
  • The output is a normal ELF executable, indistinguishable in shape from a C program built with GCC for that CPU.

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text: The compiler, stenopos, is also the formatter, linter, doc generator, test runner and language server, so there are no extra tools to install. This page covers using them on single files. In a project, tagma fmt, tagma lint, tagma doc and tagma test run the same tools over all of its sources (see Projects with tagma).

docs.title: stenopos fmt
docs.text:
Format source to the canonical style: 4-space indentation by brace depth, trimmed trailing whitespace, collapsed blank runs, and a single trailing newline. Comments and string contents are preserved exactly.

stenopos fmt src/main.sten          # reformat in place
stenopos fmt --check src/*.sten     # report unformatted files, exit 1 (for CI)

Formatting is idempotent — running it on already-formatted code changes nothing.

docs.title: stenopos lint
docs.text:
Report style and correctness lints over the parsed source.

stenopos lint src/*.sten

The current checks cover naming conventions (snake_case for functions and parameters, PascalCase for types and enum variants) and flag empty function bodies. Exit code is 1 if any lints are found.

docs.title: stenopos doc
docs.text:
Generate a Markdown API reference for a module's public surface — its pub functions, structs, enums, traits, and type aliases, with full signatures and the prose from their /// doc comments.

stenopos doc src/vector.sten              # print to stdout
stenopos doc src/vector.sten -o vector.md # write a file

/// Computes the area of a circle given its radius.
pub func circle_area(float64 radius) -> float64 {
    return 3.14159 * radius * radius
}

renders the signature followed by "Computes the area of a circle given its radius."

docs.title: stenopos test
docs.text:
Discover the @test functions in a file, run them, and report pass/fail.

// math_test.sten
func add(int32 a, int32 b) -> int32 { return a + b }

@test
func test_add() -> void {
    if (add(2, 3) != 5) {
        fail("add(2, 3) should be 5")
    }
}

stenopos test math_test.sten
# running 1 test(s) from math_test.sten
# test test_add ...
# ok — 1 test(s) passed

A test signals failure by aborting (for example via fail); the runner reports a non-zero exit when any test fails.

docs.title: Seeing the generated code
docs.text:
stenopos emit-ir src/main.sten main.ll   # the LLVM IR the compiler produces

Coming

dump-tokens and dump-ast (the lexer's tokens and the parsed tree), and --verify-ir (a structural check of the generated IR) were tools of the earlier Rust compiler and haven't been rebuilt yet.

docs.title: stenopos explain
docs.text:
Every diagnostic is tagged with an error code — error[E0300]: .... Pass that code to stenopos explain for a long-form explanation of the whole class of problem, with guidance on how to fix it:

stenopos explain E0300

E0300 [type error]

The expected type does not match the actual type. Stenopos does not
perform implicit type conversions. Use `cast[T]()` for safe numeric
conversions or `.to_X()` methods for other conversions.

Codes are grouped by compiler phase: E01xx lexer, E02xx parser, E03xx type, E04xx memory/ownership, E05xx security. explain knows every standard code, so you can look one up straight from the error[...] tag in a build's output.

docs.title: stenopos lsp
docs.text:
The language server. Your editor starts it and talks to it over standard input and output using the Language Server Protocol.

  • Diagnostics come from the real type checker, run on the unsaved buffer, so they match a build exactly.
  • Hover, go to definition and completion use the compiler's own lexer, so they keep working while the file is mid-edit. They cover functions, methods, structs, classes, enums and traits, including the public names of modules the file imports.

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
A small extension that starts stenopos lsp as its server:

import { ExtensionContext } from "vscode";
import { LanguageClient, TransportKind } from "vscode-languageclient/node";

export function activate(_ctx: ExtensionContext) {
  const serverOptions = { command: "stenopos", args: ["lsp"], transport: TransportKind.stdio };
  const clientOptions = { documentSelector: [{ scheme: "file", language: "stenopos" }] };
  new LanguageClient("stenopos", "Stenopos", serverOptions, clientOptions).start();
}

Register the stenopos language for .sten files in the extension's package.json (contributes.languages).

docs.title: Effect System
docs.text:
Functions can declare what kind of effects they have, and the compiler holds them to it.

Annotation Means @pure No effects: no I/O, and it may call only other effect-bounded functions @io Performs I/O @net Uses the network 
@pure
func add(int32 a, int32 b) -> int32 {
    return a + b
}

@io
func show(int32 x) -> void {
    println("{x}")
}

A @pure function that prints, or that calls a function with no effect annotation (whose effects the compiler can't vouch for), is a compile error:

func helper() -> int32 {
    println("side effect")
    return 1
}

@pure
func p() -> int32 {
    return helper()     // error: `helper`'s effects are unverified
}

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
A @pure function can be trusted completely: a math library marked @pure can't sneak in a file or network access. Pure functions are also trivial to test and safe to run in parallel.

For access to files, processes and the network, the stronger mechanism is capabilities: @cap(...) must be declared by every function on the call path.

docs.title: Security Overview
docs.text: Stenopos makes security properties part of the type system: the compiler rejects the program, rather than a runtime check catching it later.

docs.title: What the compiler enforces today
docs.text: Dimension What it does Example Memory safety (NOVA) Automatic, leak-free memory; no use-after-free or double free; bounds-checked indexing; checked integer overflow Memory Safety Null safety Only a T? can be null, and it must be checked before use Nullable types Taint tracking Untrusted data can't reach a @sink until a @sanitizer has cleaned it Taint Tracking Capabilities A function that touches files, processes or the network must declare @cap(...), and so must everything that calls it below Effects A @pure function can't do I/O or call anything whose effects are unknown Effect System Constant time A secret[T] value can't steer a branch or a division below Contracts @requires / @ensures are checked on every call Contracts Sensitive data @sensitive values are wiped when freed below

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
@cap(File)
func save(str text) -> void {
    discard write_file("/tmp/notes.txt", text)
}

@cap(File)
func main() -> int32 {
    save("hello")
    println(read_file("/tmp/notes.txt"))
    return 0
}

Remove @cap(File) from main and the program doesn't compile: main calls save, which needs the File capability. The resources are File, Process, Network, Memory and System. A dependency can't quietly start using the network, because its callers would have to grant it.

docs.title: Constant-time secrets
docs.text:
func main() -> int32 {
    secret[int32] key = secret(42)
    secret[int32] mixed = wrapping_add(key, secret(8))
    // if (key == 42) { ... }   // error: a secret value may not drive a branch
    // key + 8                  // error: a checked `+` would branch on its overflow
    return 0
}

Arithmetic on secrets is modular: use wrapping_add, wrapping_sub and wrapping_mul. A checked +, - or * branches on its overflow, and with a secret operand that branch would leak it. Dividing by a secret, indexing with one and shifting by one are errors for the same reason.

docs.title: Sensitive data
docs.text:
func main() -> int32 {
    @sensitive str password = "hunter2"
    println(password)
    return 0
}
// the buffer holding the password is wiped before it is freed

docs.title: Coming
docs.text:
• Constant-time code generation checked in the compiler's output (today the type rules hold; the generated machine code isn't checked yet).
  • Contracts proved at compile time, not only checked at run time.
  • A misspelled annotation (@sanitiser) is currently ignored; it will be an error.

docs.title: Taint Tracking
docs.text:
Taint tracking is a compile-time data-flow analysis that prevents injection attacks. Data from an untrusted source is tainted; anything computed from tainted data is tainted too; and a sink (a function that would be dangerous with untrusted input) refuses tainted data at compile time. A sanitizer returns clean data.

import std.string.{split, join}

@tainted
func read_param() -> str {          // a source: its result is tainted
    return "x'; DROP TABLE users"
}

@sanitizer
func sql_escape(str s) -> str {     // returns clean data: doubles every quote
    return join(split(s, "'"), "''")
}

@sink
func db_query(str sql) -> void {    // refuses tainted data
    println(sql)
}

func main() -> int32 {
    str name = read_param()
    // db_query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")   // compile error
    str safe = sql_escape(name)
    db_query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{safe}'")      // ok
    return 0
}

A variable can be marked as a source directly:

@tainted str input = arg(1)

Taint flows through assignments, string interpolation, concatenation and function calls.

docs.title: What it prevents
docs.text: SQL injection, command injection, HTML/XSS injection, path traversal, and any injection into a sink you define.

Three names, one toolchain, split the way Rust's is (cargo and rustc):

Name What it is You use it to Syntagma The toolchain as a whole, and its releases Install and update tagma The build tool, and (from rc.6) the package manager Work on a project: tagma new, build, run, test stenopos The compiler, also the language server Compile one file, or embed the compiler in other tools

Most of the time you only type tagma. The language is called Stenopos, like the platform, and its files are .sten.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
• Syntagma uses semantic versions (v1.0.0-rc.5, then v1.0.0, v1.1.0). tagma and stenopos always share that version, because they are built and tested together.
  • The language changes through editions, not version numbers. A project names its edition in Tagma.toml (edition = "2026", the first). One compiler accepts every edition it knows, and breaking changes only come with a new edition that a project opts into.
  • The standard library has its own versions. Each Syntagma release bundles one, pinned.

docs.title: Release contents
docs.text: Every release is signed in CI by the Stenopos release key and ships, for each of six architectures, a bundle with both commands, the runtime and the standard library. See Downloads.

json = { package = "stenopos/json", version = "1.2", caps = [] }
yaml = { package = "alice/yaml", version = "0.3", caps = ["File"] }
  • Names are namespaced (stenopos/json), so nobody can squat a short name and you can see who owns a package. You import a package by its name (import json.{parse}) and can rename one in Tagma.toml.
  • version = "1.2" means "at least 1.2.0" in the 1.x line.

docs.title: Dependencies only get the powers you grant
docs.text: Every package's capabilities (File, Network, Process…) are computed when it is published. In Tagma.toml you grant each dependency the capabilities it may use. If a new version of a JSON library suddenly wants Network, your build fails and names the package, instead of quietly giving it network access. A package can only pass on to its own dependencies what it was granted itself, and the compiler enforces the limit on the package's code.

docs.title: Predictable versions
docs.text: tagma uses minimal version selection: for each package it takes the highest of the minimum versions anything asks for, and never a newer version that nobody asked for. Versions only move when you run tagma update or tagma add. Tagma.lock records exactly what was chosen.

docs.title: Integrity and trust
docs.text:
• The registry is a signed index (a git repository) recording each version's source commit and a hash of its files. It does not host code.
  • tagma checks that hash before compiling anything, and Tagma.lock records it, so every later build verifies against it.
  • The index carries a signed snapshot with a seven-day expiry, so an old or frozen copy of the index is detected.
  • Every version is signed by its publisher, and the registry's root key is kept offline.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command What it does tagma add <pkg>[@<version>] Add a dependency tagma remove <pkg> Remove one tagma update [<pkg>] Move to newer versions tagma publish Publish a version (the Stenopos organization first) tagma vendor Copy dependencies into vendor/ for offline builds --locked, --offline Fail if Tagma.lock would change; never use the network

The standard library is not a registry package: it ships with Syntagma.

--feature NAME turns on @cfg(feature == "NAME") code.

docs.title: Tagma.toml
docs.text:
[package]
name = "hello"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2026"

[dependencies]
util = { path = "../util" }
  • name: letters, digits, - and _, starting with a letter.
  • version: the project's own semantic version.
  • edition: the language edition the project is written in.

A program's entry point is src/main.sten; a library's is src/lib.sten. check, test and doc work on both; build and run need a src/main.sten.

docs.title: Build profiles
docs.text: tagma build makes a draft build: fast to compile and easy to debug. tagma build --release makes an optimized, stripped build that reads like a generic C binary. Every build is hardened: position-independent, full RELRO, a non-executable stack and stack protection.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Today a dependency is a local path to another project. Its src/ directory becomes an import root:

util/src/lib.sten        module util ... pub func greet(str who) -> str
hello/src/main.sten      import util.{greet}

Dependencies from the package registry (tagma add) arrive in rc.6; see Packages and the registry. Until then tagma refuses them with a clear error.

docs.text:
// tests/math.sten
@test
func adds() -> void {
    if (1 + 1 != 2) {
        fail("math is broken")
    }
}

tagma test

docs.title: Single files
docs.text: stenopos keeps its single-file commands (stenopos run file.sten, build, check, fmt, lint, doc, test). Inside a project, it points you to tagma instead.

docs.title: Stenopos OS
docs.text:
Designed

Stenopos OS is a memory-safe, capability-based operating system written in Stenopos. It is designed to be the hardest place for an attack to get through, while still running the world's software: native .pano apps, Debian packages through apt-get, and Windows .exe programs, on hardware from Raspberry Pis to servers and phones.

Designed, not yet built

The design is complete and recorded in architecture decision records. Building starts with the foundations (see the roadmap). These pages explain the design.

docs.title: The design in brief
docs.text:
• A small verified core. The nucleus (L0) is the only code with full control of the hardware, and it is formally verified.
  • Everything else in compartments. Drivers, filesystems, the network stack and the syscall layer each run in their own hardware-isolated compartment. A bug in one cannot reach the others.
  • No root. All authority is capabilities: specific, delegable and revocable. Administration is a scoped grant you confirm on a trusted path.
  • An immutable system. The system image is verified at boot, updated atomically, and rolled back automatically if an update fails.
  • Apps get what they declare. Each app lists the capabilities it needs, and nothing else is reachable.
  • Honest about hardware. The OS reports the security tier the hardware allows and never weakens protection silently.
