docs.title: Boot, updates and firmware
docs.text: Designed

docs.title: Chain of trust
docs.text:
Every piece of code that runs with system authority is verified before it runs and measured into a hardware root of trust (a TPM where present).

  • The system lives on an immutable, hash-verified image with two slots (A and B) and anti-rollback.
  • If a stage fails verification, the device falls back to the other slot. If both fail, it boots a signed recovery image (Phoenix). It never boots unverified code silently.
  • Stenopos OS signs with its own keys, and the device owner can enroll their own keys through a deliberate, physically present, measured action.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
• Every official artifact (system images, packages, runtimes) is reproducibly built, signed by a threshold of keys, and recorded in a public append-only transparency log. Devices refuse anything that is not in the log, and policy can require independent rebuilds to agree.
  • System images update by signed A/B delta updates and roll back automatically if the new image fails.
  • Compartments, drivers and services update live, without a reboot.
  • Security updates install automatically by default.
  • Channels: Nightly, Beta, Stable and LTS (five years or more).

docs.title: Firmware: Krepis
docs.text:
Krepis updates device firmware: UEFI, SSDs, Thunderbolt and USB controllers, docks, peripherals, embedded controllers and the Raspberry Pi EEPROM, using the LVFS catalogue and UEFI capsules.

  • Every image is checked twice: the vendor's signature and Krepis policy.
  • Each device is flashed by its own sandboxed plugin, and the result is recorded in the measured boot state.
  • Flashing always needs the owner's approval and passes pre-flight checks (power, free storage, device health). A/B firmware slots are used where the hardware supports them.
  • Platform controls (battery, thermal, fans, sensors, lid and dock) are capability-scoped interfaces. Servers are managed through Redfish.

docs.title: Capabilities and services
docs.text: Designed

docs.title: No root
docs.text:
Stenopos OS has no superuser. No account, process or service holds unlimited authority. All authority is a capability: an unforgeable, specific reference to one resource with specific rights, which can be delegated and revoked.

  • Administration is a grant. An administrative action is a scoped, optionally time-limited capability, confirmed through a trusted path that software cannot fake.
  • Apps are sandboxed by default. An app declares the capabilities it needs in its manifest; you approve them, often at first use, and nothing else is reachable.
  • Powerboxes. To open a file, an app asks the system file chooser; only the file you pick is passed to it.
  • Legacy software that expects root runs against a virtualized root holding only what it was granted.

docs.title: Services and IPC
docs.text:
All communication between processes, services and compartments uses typed channels that carry capabilities.

  • Interfaces are declared in Stenopos (interface blocks). The compiler generates bindings and a zero-copy wire format that is validated in place.
  • Three transports cover every need: a synchronous fast-path call, asynchronous channels (chan[T]), and shared-memory rings.
  • There is no global service registry. A service is reachable only if a component's manifest routes a capability to it.
  • Interfaces are versioned, with evolution rules the compiler checks.
  • D-Bus (for Linux apps) and COM/RPC (for Windows apps) are bridged.

Ephor, the init and service manager, starts, watches and restarts every service. What each service can reach is set by the capability routing in its manifest, not by Ephor's own authority.

docs.title: Running other software
docs.text:
Lx: Designed Nx: Designed Xt: Designed Xenia: Designed Oikos: Designed

Stenopos OS runs the software people already have, without letting it weaken the system.

You have… It runs on… Notes A native app (Stenopos, C, C++, Rust, Go, …) The native ABI Every language gets the same sandbox A .deb or apt-get Lx A virtualized root; no Linux kernel A Docker or OCI image Oikos on Lx No shared Linux kernel A Windows .exe or .msi Nx A virtualized Administrator An x86 program on ARM or RISC-V Xt Translated ahead of time and cached Something that needs a real Linux or Windows kernel An opt-in VM (Xenia) Labelled lower assurance

docs.title: Linux: Lx
docs.text: Lx is a memory-safe Stenopos server that implements the Linux user-space interface, so unmodified Linux binaries run with no Linux kernel present. Distributions such as Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora run as isolated environments, where dpkg and apt-get work normally against a virtualized root. For software that needs a real kernel (kernel modules, eBPF, exotic system calls), a genuine Linux kernel can run in a lightweight VM, clearly labelled as lower assurance.

docs.title: Windows: Nx
docs.text: Nx is a native Windows personality written in Stenopos. It implements the NT system interface and the Win32 API surface (kernel32, user32, gdi32, advapi32, ntdll, the DirectX family and more) directly on Stenopos capabilities. It is not built on Wine or on Lx. A real Windows VM remains available, opt-in, for software that truly needs a Windows kernel.

docs.title: x86 on ARM and RISC-V: Xt
docs.text: Xt runs x86-64 and 32-bit x86 programs on ARM64 and RISC-V hosts. It translates ahead of time at install, caching the result, with a JIT fallback for code generated at run time. Translated programs call native Stenopos implementations of system libraries directly, so only the program's own code is translated. Xt is shared by Lx and Nx.

docs.title: Virtual machines and containers
docs.text:
• Xenia runs full guest operating systems on L0's hypervisor. Each VM's device model is a memory-safe Stenopos compartment of its own. Confidential VMs (AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX, Arm CCA), live migration and IOMMU passthrough are supported.
  • Oikos provides native capability-confined containers, and runs unmodified OCI and Docker images on Lx without a Linux kernel.
  • A Kubernetes-compatible node agent lets Stenopos machines join existing clusters.
  • Stenopos OS also runs well as a guest on KVM, Hyper-V, VMware and Xen.

docs.title: Native apps in any language
docs.text: All system components are written in Stenopos, but third-party apps may be written in any language. The OS interfaces are declared in Stenopos, and the toolchain generates typed bindings for C, C++, Rust, Zig, Go, Swift, Python, JavaScript and TypeScript, and C#. Apps written in memory-safe languages earn a verified "memory-safe" badge; C and C++ apps are built with mandatory hardening.

docs.title: Cryptography and verification
docs.text: Designed

docs.title: Skytale
docs.text:
All cryptography in Stenopos OS comes from Skytale, a Stenopos library whose primitives are formally verified for functional correctness, memory safety and constant-time execution.

  • Constant time is enforced by the language's secret[T] type: a secret value cannot steer a branch or a memory access.
  • The default suite is hybrid post-quantum: a classical and a post-quantum algorithm together, so breaking one is not enough.
  • Every stored crypto object carries a suite identifier, so algorithms can be replaced without guesswork.
  • Private keys live in an isolated key-service compartment, backed by hardware where available.
  • Apps get a misuse-resistant high-level API. The system TLS stack is TLS 1.3 only.

docs.title: How the core is proved correct
docs.text:
• Compiler-integrated verification. Contracts, invariants, ghost code and lemmas are written in Stenopos and checked by an SMT solver on every build.
  • A formal semantics of Stenopos in Lean 4. The verifier and the type system (memory safety, taint, secret[T]) are proved sound against it.
  • Translation validation. For L0 and Skytale, the compiled machine code is checked against the verified source, closing the gap a compiler bug could open.

docs.title: Graphics and desktop
docs.text: Eikon: Designed Skene: Designed Stenopos Desktop: Designed Morphe: Designed

docs.title: Eikon and Skene
docs.text:
• Eikon is the one native, explicit graphics API, and the only API GPU drivers implement. Vulkan, OpenGL, Direct3D 9 to 12 and the UI toolkit are all built on it. Every app gets an isolated GPU context.
  • Skene, the compositor, runs in its own compartment and treats windows, input, screen capture, the clipboard and hotkeys as capabilities. No app can log keys, scrape the screen or read the clipboard unless granted.
  • Skene draws a trusted UI that apps cannot imitate: the real identity of the app you are using, trusted-path prompts, and privacy indicators for the camera, microphone and screen sharing.
  • Linux (Wayland and X11) and Windows apps are bridged onto Skene, each confined separately.

docs.title: Stenopos Desktop
docs.text:
The desktop is inspired by GNOME by default (a top bar, an overview, a dash and dynamic workspaces) and ships five layouts: Activities, Classic, Dock, Tiling and Tablet.

Customization comes in three levels:

  1. Themes, which are data and never code.
  2. Layouts and panels, composed from parts.
  3. Extensions, which are signed, sandboxed .pano processes using a capability-scoped API, not code injected into the shell.

Morphe, the native UI toolkit, renders through Eikon and exposes an accessibility tree for every widget. Accessibility is first-class, and so is internationalization: UTF-8 everywhere with spoofing detection, complex scripts, right-to-left layouts, and sandboxed input methods.

docs.title: Drivers and peripherals
docs.text: Kanon: Designed Peripheral Guard: Designed

docs.title: The driver model
docs.text:
Every device driver is native Stenopos code in its own compartment, holding only its device's capabilities: its registers, its interrupts and DMA buffers confined by the IOMMU.

  • Kanon, a device description language, declares registers and DMA formats. Type-safe register accessors and DMA validators are generated from it, so a driver cannot write a malformed command.
  • Drivers plug into bus drivers and typed class interfaces, connected by ownership-tracked shared-memory rings.
  • Drivers are restartable after a crash and live-updatable.
  • Linux and Windows kernel drivers never run on the host.

docs.title: Peripheral Guard
docs.text:
Peripheral Guard treats every newly connected device as untrusted.

  • A device's interfaces are listed but not bound to drivers until you authorize them, one interface at a time.
  • A new keyboard or mouse needs human confirmation, which defeats "USB rubber ducky" attacks.
  • Nothing new is enabled while the screen is locked.
  • Thunderbolt and USB4 devices that tunnel PCIe get their own IOMMU domain and an explicit authorization.
  • Charge-only mode defeats juice jacking.
  • Apps reach devices only through per-device capabilities. Kiosk and embedded systems can lock port policy with a signed policy.

docs.title: Identity, logs and recovery
docs.text: Designed

docs.title: Login and identity
docs.text:
• Local first. Accounts live on the device; no cloud account is ever required. Federation (OIDC, SAML, Active Directory-compatible) is optional.
  • Phishing-resistant unlock. A device-bound key, unlocked by a PIN that the hardware rate-limits, by biometrics matched in an isolated compartment, or by a FIDO2 security key. Passwords remain an option, never the only one.
  • A built-in passkey provider.
  • Login releases your disk keys, and happens on the trusted path.
  • One capability-scoped secrets store serves every app.
  • Recovery uses keys you hold, optionally split among people you trust (m of n). There is no backdoor.

docs.title: Logs and audit
docs.text:
• A tamper-evident security audit log: hash-chained, signed and anchored in the TPM, and optionally streamed off the device.
  • Structured diagnostic logs that cost nothing when not read.
  • Secrets are redacted by the type system: a @secret or @sensitive value cannot reach a log.
  • Reading logs needs a scoped, read-only capability. It can be granted to others (an "Observer" role, for example) with user activity pseudonymized by default, and every read is itself audited.
  • Crash reports stay on the device unless you send them.
  • Debugging another process needs a debug capability granted on the trusted path. Tracing uses static, verified probe points, never injected kernel code.

docs.title: Phoenix, recovery mode
docs.text: Phoenix is the signed recovery image. If the system fails verification at boot, the device first falls back to the other system slot; if both fail, it boots Phoenix rather than any unverified code. From there a broken system can be repaired or restored, for example from a Thesauros backup. What else the recovery image contains is still being designed.

docs.title: Kernel and compartments
docs.text:
Agoge: Designed L0 nucleus: Designed

The kernel, Agoge, is compartmentalized. It is neither a monolith, where one driver bug compromises everything, nor a classic microkernel, where every call pays for a context switch.

docs.title: The layers
docs.text:
Layer What runs there L0, the nucleus Address translation, DMA control, interrupts, privileged registers and capabilities. Formally verified, running at the hardware's highest privilege level (hypervisor level: VMX root, EL2 or HS mode) L1 Drivers, one compartment each, restartable L2 Storage: Stoa and foreign filesystems L3 Networking: Dromos L4 The syscall broker, the only door from user space

Compartments run with kernel-class performance, but they cannot read or write each other's memory, cannot DMA outside the buffers granted to them, and can only call L0 through capability-checked gates.

Every compartment is placement-agnostic: the same source can be built as an isolated kernel compartment (fast) or as a user process (maximum isolation), chosen per component.

docs.title: Security tiers
docs.text:
Stenopos OS runs on x86-64, ARM64 and RISC-V from the first line of code. At boot, L0 probes what the hardware actually offers and picks the strongest isolation available for each job. The machine then runs at a declared security tier, reported to you and to software. Policy can refuse to run sensitive work below a required tier.

At build time, an architecture and platform profile selects what is compiled in; code for anything else is left out of the image entirely.

docs.title: Scheduling and power
docs.text: CPU time is a capability too. L0 implements only the verified mechanism: scheduling contexts (a budget per period, core affinity) with time donated across IPC. A separate policy compartment decides budgets: fair interactive scheduling, declared quality-of-service classes, and admission-controlled real time. Scheduling is per core, tickless, and aware of mixed big and little cores and of energy. High-security work can opt into time protection: core partitioning, cache colouring and flushing on switch.

docs.title: Audio, media and printing
docs.text: Aulos: Designed Lyra: Designed Opsis: Designed Typos: Designed

docs.title: Aulos, audio
docs.text:
Aulos is one native, low-latency audio graph for everyday and professional use alike. It runs in its own compartment, starts on demand, and uses real-time scheduling and zero-copy rings.

  • Playback, recording, and capturing other apps' audio are separate capabilities.
  • The microphone indicator cannot be suppressed.
  • Hardware: HD Audio, USB Audio, I²S, HDMI and DisplayPort, and Bluetooth including LE Audio. Linux and Windows audio APIs are bridged.

docs.title: Lyra and Opsis, media and camera
docs.text:
Lyra is the media framework behind the media player.

  • Files and streams are parsed by memory-safe Stenopos parsers in short-lived decoder sandboxes with no capabilities. A malicious video file has nothing to attack.
  • Hardware acceleration is isolated, and there is a zero-copy path from the network to the display.
  • Royalty-free codecs are built in. Patent-encumbered ones use the device's licensed hardware decoder or an opt-in codec package.
  • DRM is optional and confined.

Opsis is the camera pipeline (USB and MIPI cameras and the image processor), gated by capability, with an indicator that cannot be suppressed.

docs.title: Typos, printing and scanning
docs.text:
Typos is driverless first: IPP Everywhere (compatible with AirPrint and Mopria) for printing, and eSCL and WSD for scanning.

  • There is no listening print daemon by default. Network printers are discovered outbound and added only when you confirm.
  • Each job is rendered in a throwaway sandbox with no capabilities.
  • Legacy printer filters run as sandboxed components.
  • Apps print through a trusted print dialog, and see only what you send.

docs.title: Networking and Phalanx
docs.text: Dromos: Designed Phalanx: Designed

docs.title: Dromos
docs.text:
Dromos is the native network stack, split across compartments.

  • Packet parsing is isolated from transport state, and all packet data is treated as tainted by the compiler.
  • Network access is a capability. Apps declare the endpoints they need. Inbound is denied by default; outbound is granted per app.
  • Local-network access is a separate capability, so an app that may reach the internet cannot scan your home network.
  • The system resolver validates DNSSEC over encrypted DNS.
  • A built-in WireGuard-compatible VPN uses a hybrid post-quantum handshake and supports per-app routing.
  • Insecure legacy protocols are never supported on the host.

docs.title: Phalanx
docs.text:
Phalanx is the security center: one place for network access and the firewall, malware scanning, and the audit log.

Phalanx Scan checks files on arrival (downloads, mail attachments, removable media, and files in Linux and Windows environments), on a schedule and on demand.

  • Every scan runs in a short-lived sandbox with no capabilities, so a malicious file cannot exploit the scanner.
  • It reads YARA rules and ClamAV signatures.
  • It is private by default: nothing is uploaded.
  • It never hooks into the kernel.

docs.title: Packages: Panoplia and .pano
docs.text:
Designed

Native software for Stenopos OS ships as a .pano: a signed, declarative, content-addressed bundle with a capability manifest and no install scripts. Panoplia (pano) installs and updates them.

pano install laconic
pano update
pano remove laconic

docs.title: What makes it safe
docs.text:
• Declarative. A package says what it contains and what it needs; it cannot run code at install time, so installing an app cannot change the system.
  • Capabilities declared up front. The manifest lists the capabilities the app uses and exposes. You see them before you install.
  • An immutable store. Installed packages live in a hash-verified, content-addressed store. Upgrades are atomic and rollback is instant.
  • Shared runtimes. Apps depend on signed, versioned runtimes that are patched centrally. An app may bundle private libraries; they are flagged and scanned for known vulnerabilities.
  • Open distribution. The official repository, third-party repositories and signed sideloading are all supported. You decide whom to trust.

.pano combines three proven ideas: capability-native components (as in Fuchsia and WASI), a functional content-addressed store (as in Nix and Guix), and sandboxed bundles with shared runtimes (as in Flatpak).

Every first-party app is an ordinary .pano: removable and replaceable.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Minimal memory use and maximum speed are requirements for every component, on the same footing as correctness, and never achieved by weakening security.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.text:
Each metric has a target (the goal) and a hard ceiling: at most half of the leanest mainstream operating system on the same hardware, measured in CI. Missing a target needs a written justification; missing a ceiling blocks the release.

Metric Profile Target Image size Embedded ≤ 16 MiB RAM Embedded, minimal device ≤ 32 MiB Idle RAM Server ≤ 128 MiB Idle RAM Raspberry Pi desktop ≤ 300 MiB Idle RAM Laptop and desktop ≤ 400 MiB Minimum RAM Laptop and desktop 1 GiB (ceiling 2 GiB) Boot to login, after firmware Laptop and desktop (NVMe) ≤ 3 s Boot to ready, after firmware Server ≤ 2 s Driver crash recovery All ≤ 1 s Linux and Windows compatibility overhead, CPU-bound All ≤ 2% Translated x86-64 speed ARM64 and RISC-V ≥ 70% of native

docs.title: Optimizations that are forbidden
docs.text:
Some well-known speed-ups open security holes, so Stenopos OS never uses them:

Optimization Why not Instead Deduplicating writable memory across domains Enables side-channel and Rowhammer attacks Share only immutable, public, signed content Turning off speculative-execution mitigations at trust boundaries Reopens Spectre-class leaks The cheapest correct mitigation per CPU Skipping validation for "trusted" senders Confused-deputy attacks In-place validation, which is nearly free Shared address spaces between trust domains Breaks isolation Hardware gates and shared rings Unencrypted swap or cross-domain memory compression Leaks secrets Encrypted swap and per-domain compression JIT compilation in the trusted core Breaks W^X and verification Ahead-of-time compilation everywhere

docs.title: Storage and backup
docs.text: Stoa: Designed Thesauros: Designed

docs.title: Stoa, the filesystem
docs.text:
Stoa is the native filesystem, written in Stenopos and running in its own storage compartment.

  • Copy-on-write with an end-to-end cryptographic Merkle tree: every block is verified when read.
  • Per-file authenticated encryption, with a key hierarchy per user, per app and per environment. Your keys are released when you log in.
  • Instant, immutable snapshots.
  • Capabilities, not permission bits. Access is granted by capability; there are no permission bits or ACLs acting as authority.
  • Deduplication and compression, tuned for flash and NVMe.
  • Foreign filesystems are read by native drivers, each in its own compartment.

docs.title: Thesauros, backup and sync
docs.text:
Thesauros backs up by sending incremental Stoa snapshot streams.

  • Always end-to-end encrypted and Merkle-verified.
  • To any destination: an external disk, a NAS, another Stenopos machine, or S3-compatible storage.
  • Destinations are written through append-only capabilities, so ransomware on the machine cannot delete or overwrite its backups.
  • Restore a file, an app or a user, or a whole device, even onto a different CPU architecture.
  • Optional device-to-device sync, end-to-end encrypted and peer-to-peer, with no vendor in the trust path.

docs.title: The Stenopos platform
docs.text:
In progress

Stenopos is an operating system, the language it is written in, the toolchain that builds it, and a suite of apps, all designed together around one rule: security above all (Ἀσφάλεια περὶ πλείστου).

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
Every design decision is measured against five principles:

  1. Best first: no interim architectures. Each part is built to its final design. Work can be sequenced, but nothing is a throwaway stepping stone.
  2. Security is never silently degraded. When hardware or software can't meet a guarantee, the system says so: security tiers, attestation state and assurance labels.
  3. The owner stays in control. Open distribution, owner-enrolled keys, no walled garden. Every trust decision is explicit and recorded.
  4. Least privilege everywhere. No root and no ambient authority: capabilities from the nucleus up to every app.
  5. Fast and lean, never at the cost of security. Memory use and speed are design requirements with budgets enforced in CI, and security is never traded for them.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Apps: native .pano (any language) · Linux (Lx) · Windows (Nx)        │
│ Browsers · containers (Oikos) · x86 translation (Xt)                 │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Desktop: Stenopos Desktop · Morphe · Skene · Eikon                   │
│ Services: audio · media · printing · firmware · identity · backup    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ L4  Syscall broker: the only door from user space                    │
│ L3  Network (Dromos)          L2  Storage (Stoa)                     │
│ L1  Drivers: one compartment each, restartable                       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ L0  Nucleus: formally verified, at hypervisor level                  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Verified and measured boot · immutable A/B system image              │
│ Hardware: x86-64 · ARM64 · RISC-V                                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Everything above the hardware is written in the Stenopos language. The language's own safety checks (memory safety, taint tracking, effects, capabilities and constant-time secrets) are what make it practical to write an OS this way.

docs.title: The names
docs.text:
Every Stenopos product is named from the world of ancient Sparta and Greece. This page explains what each name means, how to say it, and why it fits.

Ἀσφάλεια περὶ πλείστου (aspháleia perì pleístou): "Security above all."

docs.title: The platform: Stenopos
docs.text:
Greek Στενωπός (stenōpós) Say it STEN-oh-pos Meaning "The narrow pass"

In 480 BC, King Leonidas and 300 Spartans held the pass of Thermopylae against the vast army of Persia. They didn't win by being more numerous. They won by choosing the narrow pass: the enemy could only come through one small opening, and that opening was defended.

That is the Stenopos security design in one image: - Minimize the attack surface. Everything must come through a few narrow, capability-checked gates. - A small, verified core (the nucleus) holds against everything else. - Nothing gets through by default. No root, no ambient authority.

"Stenopos" names the whole platform: the operating system (Stenopos OS), the programming language and compiler (Stenopos), and the family of products below.

docs.title: The mark
docs.text: The platform's symbol is a golden Spartan (Corinthian) helmet with a red crest, inside a bronze ring. The helmet stands for the hoplite who holds the line: protection first, which is what the platform is built around.

docs.title: The motto
docs.text: Ἀσφάλεια περὶ πλείστου (aspháleia perì pleístou): "Security above all." It is the one motto of the whole platform, and the rule every design decision is measured against.

Stenopos OS is built in eight phases. Each ends in something you can run, and none of them is a throwaway design: a phase decides the order, and every component is built to its final architecture.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text: Stenopos is designed so that a bug in one part cannot become control of the whole system, and so that every grant of power is explicit.

docs.title: The guarantees
docs.text: Guarantee How Details A driver, filesystem or network bug cannot take over the system Each runs in its own hardware-isolated compartment with its own IOMMU domain Kernel, Drivers The core is correct The nucleus, the crypto library and the filesystem are formally verified Verification Nothing tampered with boots Verified and measured boot, the owner's own keys, anti-rollback Boot No all-powerful account No root; capabilities only; grants confirmed on a trusted path Capabilities Installing an app cannot change the system .pano packages have no install scripts and live in an immutable store Packages Apps get only what they declare and you approve Capability manifests, first-use prompts, powerboxes Capabilities No keylogging, screen scraping or fake dialogs Input, capture and windows are capabilities; a trusted UI apps cannot draw Desktop No silent network access Per-app network capabilities, default deny Networking Your data is unreadable without you Per-file encryption with keys released at login Storage, Identity Crypto is correct and constant-time Verified primitives; secret[T] in the type system; hybrid post-quantum Cryptography Updates cannot be secretly poisoned Reproducible builds, threshold signing, a public transparency log Updates Logs cannot be quietly erased A hash-chained, signed audit log Logs Plugged-in devices cannot attack you Peripheral Guard authorizes every new device and interface Peripherals Ransomware cannot destroy backups Append-only backup destinations and immutable snapshots Backup

docs.title: In the language
docs.text:
The same ideas start in the compiler, so code is safe before it ever runs:

Dimension What the compiler checks Memory (NOVA) Ownership states (Declared, Owned, Moved, Borrowed, Locked, Freed): no use-after-free, no double free, no data races Null safety Only T? can be empty, and it must be checked Taint Untrusted input cannot reach a sink without a sanitizer Effects and capabilities @cap(File), @cap(Network)… a function cannot do what it doesn't declare Contracts @requires and @ensures Constant time secret[T] values cannot steer branches or memory access Integer overflow Checked by default; wrapping only when asked for

See the language security overview.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• tagma, the build tool (ADR-0038). Syntagma now ships two commands: tagma for projects and stenopos, the compiler, for single files. tagma new, build, run, check, test, fmt, lint, doc and clean work on a directory with a Tagma.toml ([package] name, version and edition, plus local path [dependencies]). tagma calls the compiler's modules in-process and shares its version. The easter-egg commands moved from stenopos to tagma. See docs/TAGMA.md.
  • Editions. edition = "2026" in Tagma.toml names the language edition; the compiler refuses editions it does not know.
  • Release bundles. Each release ships syntagma-<version>-linux-<arch>.tar.gz (bin/tagma, bin/stenopos, lib/stenopos/ with the runtime and std) for all six architectures, plus standalone tagma-linux-<arch> binaries. The installer installs the bundle.
  • std.lock pins the std commit a release bundles and CI dogfoods, instead of choosing std by date.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• selfhost/ is now compiler/, and its modules are compiler.*.
  • The compiler finds its runtime and std beside its own binary (<prefix>/lib/stenopos/), so an install anywhere works without STENOPOS_HOME.
  • Inside a project, stenopos new and stenopos build/run/test without a file point to tagma.

  • The installer moved to public/install.sh (the one served from GitHub).

  • Generic structs as function return and parameter types. func make() -> Box[int32] and func f(Box[int32] b) now work (both were a clean error / silent int32). Generic struct templates are pre-registered before the signature pre-pass, so the concrete instance resolves in both collect_signatures and the body parse (parse_func/ parse_method); return Box { .. } resolves the generic literal against the declared return type. Forward references, methods, and multi-arg generics (Pair[int32, str]) all work, valgrind-clean. examples/generic_return.sten.

  • Conditional compilation: @cfg(...). A parse-time gate on top-level declarations, selected by build config — @cfg(target_arch == "x86_64"), @cfg(ptr_width == "64"), @cfg(profile == "release"), @cfg(feature == "debug"), with &&/||/! and ==/!=. Unlike a const-gated if (stripped only by the release optimizer, and still type-checked), @cfg is evaluated in the parser in BOTH passes, so an excluded declaration is never parsed, type-checked, or registered — enabling genuinely platform-specific code (e.g. x86_64-only inline asm invalid on aarch64), and two same-named @cfg variants coexist with no duplicate-definition error. Config comes from --target (arch/os/endian/ptr_width), --release (profile), and the new repeatable --feature NAME / --define NAME. examples/cfg_select.sten.
  • Top-level const globals. const int32 W = 10 (and int64/uint32/ float64/bool/str) at file scope declares a named, immutable, compile-time literal constant visible to every function in the file. It is substituted in place at each use — no storage, no indirection — so a global const name is never an assignable slot. Initializers must be a literal of the declared type; a computed expression or a type mismatch is a clean error. A local may shadow a global const. examples/const_globals.sten.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Block-local variables are now correctly scoped. A name declared inside a block ({ } of an if/while/for/do/try/with/match/unsafe) was leaking out — a nested int32 x = 2 overwrote an outer x, and the inner binding stayed visible after the block. Now a nested declaration is local to its block: shadowing is restored on block exit, sibling blocks reuse names freely, and using a block-local after its block is undefined variable. Implemented WITHOUT popping names (a block-horizon stack + a sparse dead-set), so slots stay monotonic and the const/color/codegen paths are unchanged. examples/scoping.sten. (Follow-up: reject same-scope redeclaration.)
  • Passing a fixed array directly to a slice parameter is now a clean error. f(a) where a: int32[3] and f takes int32[] used to be accepted but read garbage (.len() returned 1) and segfaulted on iteration — a fixed array is not a {len,ptr} slice view. Slice it first: f(a[0..<3]). examples/compile-fail/array_as_slice.sten.
  • Returning a generic struct type is now a clean error, not a silent mis-compile. func make() -> Box[int32] previously either failed with a confusing parse error or (as a forward reference) silently recorded int32 and returned garbage, because the signature pre-pass runs before generic structs are registered. It now reports that the case isn't supported yet (return a concrete struct or the inner value). Full support is a generics follow-up. examples/compile-fail/generic_return_type.sten.
  • do { ... } while (cond) is now implemented. It previously parsed but emitted NOTHING — the body and everything after it in the function silently vanished. It now compiles to a proper bottom-checked loop (the body runs at least once, the condition is tested at the bottom; break/continue work), and a do not followed by while (cond) is a clean parse error. examples/do_while.sten.
  • Reassigning a nullable struct/str field no longer emits ill-typed IR. t.left = insert(t.left, v) where left: Tree? stored a raw pointer into the {i1, ptr} nullable slot (rejected by llc), which blocked linked lists and trees built by field mutation. The assignment now widens a bare T -> T? (and drops the replaced inner, null-safe), so building and overwriting are both valgrind-clean. examples/bst_mutate.sten.
  • A local const declaration no longer silently drops its initializer. const int32 x = 42 previously parsed but left x empty (the const modifier was never consumed, so the declaration mis-parsed); const is now a recognized declaration modifier and the value is kept.
  • const immutability is now enforced. Reassigning a const — local (const int32 x = 1 then x = 2) or global (W = 5 on a top-level const, which used to crash with an out-of-bounds write) — is a clean compile error. Covers = and the compound forms. examples/compile-fail/const_reassign.sten.
  • A struct literal naming an unknown field is now rejected. Point { x: 1, zz: 9 } where zz is not a field previously mapped the stray value to field 0 (silently overwriting x); it now reports "struct 'Point' has no field 'zz'" (the field-index lookup returned 0 on a miss). examples/compile-fail/struct_lit_unknown_field.sten.
  • Calling an rwlock-only method on a mutex/spinlock (or vice versa) is now a clean error. m.read_lock() on a mutex[T] previously type-checked and emitted a nonsensical call; the parser now validates each lock method against its lock kind (lock/unlock for mutex/spinlock, read_lock/write_lock for rwlock, acquire/release for semaphore) and reports e.g. "mutex has no method read_lock". examples/compile-fail/lock_bad_method.sten.
  • sort() on a List whose element has no natural order is now a clean error. .sort() on a List[struct] (or a float/bool/enum list) previously fell through to the 4-byte sort_i32 path and read each element at the wrong width — a silent mis-compile. It now reports "sort needs an int32, int64, or str element type". examples/compile-fail/list_sort_struct.sten.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-alpha.1 Released
docs.text: The first alpha release of the Stenopos compiler is here. This marks a major milestone: the complete modular rewrite now compiles programs end-to-end, from source code all the way to a linked binary.

docs.title: What is Stenopos?
docs.text: Stenopos is a memory-safe, taint-aware systems programming language. It combines C-style familiarity with compile-time safety guarantees that go beyond what any existing systems language offers: memory safety, taint tracking, effect types, constant-time enforcement, and more -- all checked at compile time with zero runtime overhead.

docs.title: What works in alpha.1
docs.text:
The full compilation pipeline is operational:

Source -> Lex -> Parse -> Semantic Analysis -> IR Lowering -> LLVM Codegen -> Link -> Binary

Features you can use today:

  • Functions with parameters and return values
  • if / else control flow
  • Integer and float arithmetic
  • String literals and interpolation
  • println output
  • Type checking across the full type system
  • Borrow checking for memory safety

Here is a working Stenopos program you can compile right now:

func fibonacci(int32 n) -> int32 {
    if (n <= 1) {
        return n
    }
    return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2)
}

func main() -> int32 {
    int32 result = fibonacci(10)
    printf("fib(10) = %d\n", result)
    return 0
}

docs.title: 19-crate architecture
docs.text:
The compiler is splits into 19 independent crates, each with a clear responsibility:

Layer Crates Foundation stenopos-common, stenopos-error, stenopos-ast, stenopos-symboltable Frontend stenopos-lexer, stenopos-parser, stenopos-semantic, stenopos-security Backend stenopos-irgen, stenopos-optimizer, stenopos-codegen, stenopos-linker Runtime stenopos-runtime Tools stenopos-formatter, stenopos-lint, stenopos-tester, stenopos-doc Orchestration stenopos-driver, stenopos-cli

This structure makes each component independently testable and replaceable. It also lays the groundwork for the compiler to eventually compile itself.

docs.title: 1,307 tests passing
docs.text: The test suite covers every stage of compilation. Lexer, parser, semantic analysis, type checking, borrow checking, code generation -- all tested independently and in integration. Every commit runs the full suite.

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
The path from alpha to beta:

  • Loops: while and for loop codegen
  • More types: arrays, structs, enums
  • NOVA memory management: automatic deallocation without a garbage collector
  • Taint tracking: the security type system that makes Stenopos unique
  • Self-hosting: the compiler compiling itself

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-alpha.2 Released
docs.text: Alpha.1 could compile a program. Alpha.2 makes it a language. This release fills in the core of everyday Stenopos: a real type checker, strings that work, enums with pattern matching, and the first piece of what makes Stenopos different -- taint tracking.

docs.title: A real semantic pass
docs.text:
Alpha.1 checked types loosely. Alpha.2 adds a full second pass that actually holds the line:

  • Name resolution -- every identifier must refer to something real.
  • No implicit conversions -- an int32 is not a float64. If you want to cross that line, you say so with cast[T](). The compiler never guesses.
  • const means const -- assigning to a const is an error, not a warning.
  • Honest errors -- anything the backend can't yet compile is reported as a clear "not supported yet" error instead of silently producing a wrong program.

That last point is a rule we hold ourselves to: no miscompiles by construction. If the compiler can't do something correctly, it refuses, loudly.

docs.title: Strings that work
docs.text:
Strings now go end to end -- interpolation, concatenation, and equality:

func main() -> void {
    str name = "Stenopos"
    str greeting = "Hello, " + name
    println(greeting)
    if (name == "Stenopos") {
        println("Names match!")
    }
}

Under the hood, strings are length-prefixed {length, data} values -- not null-terminated -- backed by a small native runtime.

docs.title: Enums and match
docs.text:
Enums carry a backing type, and match checks that you handled every case:

enum Color : int32 {
    Red = 0
    Green = 1
    Blue = 2
}

func describe(Color c) -> str {
    match (c) {
        case Color.Red:   return "warm"
        case Color.Green: return "calm"
        case Color.Blue:  return "cool"
    }
}

Miss a case and the compiler tells you before your program ever runs.

docs.title: The first taste of security
docs.text: Taint tracking -- the feature that makes Stenopos Stenopos -- is now wired into the compiler. Mark where untrusted data enters (@tainted), where it gets cleaned (@sanitizer), and where it must never arrive dirty (@sink). Let tainted data reach a sink and the build fails.

docs.title: Also new
docs.text:
• break and continue in loops
  • Type-aware println (picks the right format for strings, integers, floats)
  • A constant-folding optimizer pass
  • stenopos new to scaffold a project
  • An end-to-end example suite that compiles and runs every example, checking its output -- because green unit tests once coexisted with a compiler that couldn't print "Hello".

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-alpha.3 Released
docs.text: Alpha.3 is about shapes: the ways you group data together. Structs, methods, and arrays all land in this release -- plus a subtle but important fix to how && and || behave.

docs.title: Structs
docs.text:
Group related values into a named type, read and write their fields, and nest them freely:

struct Point {
    float64 x
    float64 y
}

struct Line {
    Point start
    Point end
}

func main() -> void {
    Line l = Line {
        start: Point { x: 0.0, y: 0.0 },
        end:   Point { x: 3.0, y: 4.0 }
    }
    println("end.x = {l.end.x}")
}

Ask for a field that doesn't exist, or give one the wrong type, and it's a compile error.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Structs can carry behavior. A method takes an implicit this receiver, passed by reference -- so when a method changes a field, the change sticks:

struct Counter {
    int32 count

    pub func bump(this) -> void {
        this.count = this.count + 1
    }
}

docs.title: Fixed-size arrays -- with real bounds checks
docs.text:
Arrays get literals, indexing, and iteration. The important part: indexing is bounds-checked at runtime. Reach past the end and the program aborts with a clear message instead of quietly reading someone else's memory:

func main() -> void {
    int32[3] nums = [10, 20, 30]
    for (n in nums) {
        println("{n}")
    }
    println("first = {nums[0]}")
}

When the index is a constant the compiler can prove is in range, it skips the check -- safety where you need it, no cost where you don't.

docs.title: Short-circuit && and ||
docs.text:
Previously && and || evaluated both sides. Now they short-circuit like they should: the right side runs only when the left side doesn't already decide the answer. This matters when the right side has an effect or guards against the left:

if (p != null && p.is_ready()) { ... }   // p.is_ready() only runs when p != null

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-alpha.4 Released
docs.text: Alpha.4 is a release about releases. The headline is a compatibility fix that lets the compiler run on the machines people actually have -- plus the tooling that makes every future release something you can trust.

docs.title: Runs on the LLVM you already have
docs.text:
Stenopos emits LLVM IR and hands it to llc. The catch: LLVM changed its IR between versions, and Debian 12 and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS -- what a huge number of people run -- ship LLVM 14. Earlier alphas quietly assumed something newer.

Alpha.4 fixes this. The compiler now produces IR that links cleanly on LLVM 14 through 18:

  • it passes -opaque-pointers when it detects LLVM 14, and
  • it numbers unnamed IR values the exact way LLVM 14 insists on.

We also added a script that reproduces the precise release environment (rust:1.80 / LLVM 14) in a container, so "works on my machine" stops being a mystery.

docs.title: A one-line install
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

The installer detects your platform, downloads the right binary, and verifies its checksum before putting it on your PATH.

docs.title: Every release is proven, not promised
docs.text:
Two new habits back every release from here on:

  • The shipped binary is tested, not just the source. A public workflow downloads the actual release artifact and compiles + runs a suite of real programs against it. A status badge shows whether what you can download actually works -- independent of our private build pipeline.
  • Release notes come from the changelog. The notes you read on a release are generated straight from CHANGELOG.md, so they always match what changed.

docs.title: Why alpha.2 and alpha.3 felt quiet
docs.text: Alpha.2 and alpha.3 built the language core (semantic checking, strings, enums, structs, methods, arrays) but never fully published -- a gap in the release toolchain we've now closed. Alpha.4 bundles all of their work plus the release machinery above. If you're coming from alpha.1, you're getting everything at once.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-alpha.5 Released
docs.text: Alpha.5 is the biggest step yet toward a compiler that can compile itself. Programs can now span multiple files, arrays gained slices, structs travel through functions safely, and kernel modules get the familiar module_init / module_exit markers. Every heap-touching feature here was checked leak-free under Valgrind.

docs.title: Projects, not just files
docs.text:
Until now, a Stenopos program was a single file. Now stenopos build understands whole projects:

  • point it at a directory and it compiles every .sten beneath it,
  • point it at a stenopos.toml and it compiles that project's src/,
  • point it at a single file and it pulls in the local modules that file imports, following the chain.
// src/greeting.sten
module greeter.greeting

func greeting(str name) -> str {
    return "Hello, " + name
}

// src/main.sten
module greeter.main
import greeter.greeting.{greeting}

func main() -> void {
    println(greeting("Stenopos"))
}

stenopos build .        # or: stenopos build stenopos.toml

Both modules link into one binary. (Per-module name privacy and an incremental build cache come next; today the build merges everything into one program.)

docs.title: Slices
docs.text:
A slice is a lightweight, borrowed view into an array -- a length and a pointer, no copying:

func sum(int32[] xs) -> int32 {
    int32 total = 0
    for (x in xs) { total += x }
    return total
}

func main() -> void {
    int32[5] nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
    int32[] middle = nums[1..<4]     // a view of [20, 30, 40]
    println("len = {middle.len()}")
    println("sum = {sum(middle)}")
}

Slices support .len(), indexing (bounds-checked against the slice's own length), iteration, and passing to functions. Because a slice only borrows, slicing an array of strings copies nothing and leaks nothing.

docs.title: Structs travel safely
docs.text:
Passing a struct to a function, or returning one, now does the right thing even when the struct owns a string. A parameter is a copy the callee can change without touching the caller's value, and strings are cloned or moved so nothing is freed twice:

struct Person { str name, int32 age }

func older(Person p) -> Person {
    p.age = p.age + 1        // changes the copy only
    return p
}

docs.title: for (i, item in arr)
docs.text:
Iterate with an index and a value at once:

for (i, name in names) {
    println("{i}: {name}")
}

docs.title: Kernel modules, the familiar way
docs.text:
Stenopos can build real Linux kernel modules, and now the entry points read the way kernel developers expect. @module_init and @module_exit are shorthands that place your functions in the .init.text and .exit.text sections:

@module_init
pub func hello_init() -> int32 {
    printk("hello: loaded\n")
    return 0
}

@module_exit
pub func hello_exit() -> void {
    printk("hello: unloaded\n")
}

The general @section(".name") annotation now works too, and the section really lands in the compiled binary.

docs.title: Proven leak-free
docs.text: Owned strings, strings inside structs and arrays, break/continue cleanup, struct-by-value, and slices were all run under Valgrind on the LLVM 14 image that mirrors the release environment: zero leaks, zero errors.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-alpha.6 Released
docs.text: Alpha.6 is the "toolbox" release. It adds the data structures and text-handling a real program -- and eventually the Stenopos compiler itself -- needs: hash maps, lists of structs, string processing, character literals, and exceptions. Every heap-touching feature was checked leak-free under Valgrind.

docs.title: Hash maps
docs.text:
A string-keyed hash map, the thing every compiler's symbol table is built on:

func main() -> void {
    HashMap[str, int32] ages = map_new()
    ages.insert("alice", 30)
    ages.insert("bob", 25)
    if (ages.contains("alice")) {
        int32 a = ages.get("alice")
        println("alice is {a}")
    }
    println("entries: {ages.len()}")
}

The map owns its keys and (for string values) its values -- it clones them in and frees them when it goes out of scope. No manual cleanup, no leaks.

docs.title: Lists of structs
docs.text:
Lists already held numbers and strings. Now they hold structs too -- including structs that own strings, like a list of tokens:

struct Token {
    str text
    int32 kind
}

func main() -> void {
    List[Token] toks = list_new()
    toks.push(Token { text: "if", kind: 1 })
    println("first: {toks.get(0).text}")
}

Pushing a variable deep-copies it (your original stays valid), and every element is freed when the list is dropped.

docs.title: Reading text
docs.text:
Strings gained the operations a lexer lives on:

str s = "abc123"
println("length: {s.len()}")
int32 first = s.byte_at(0)          // 97
str head = s.substring(0, 3)        // "abc"

docs.title: Character literals
docs.text:
And characters, which are just their int32 code points -- so they compare directly with byte_at:

func is_digit(str s, int64 i) -> bool {
    int32 c = s.byte_at(i)
    return c >= '0' && c <= '9'
}

'a', '\n', '\t', '\0' all work.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
And a real error-handling path -- try / catch / finally with throw:

func checked_div(int32 a, int32 b) -> int32 {
    if (b == 0) {
        throw("division by zero")
    }
    return a / b
}

func main() -> void {
    try {
        println("{checked_div(10, 2)}")
        println("{checked_div(1, 0)}")
    } catch (Error e) {
        println("caught: {e}")
    } finally {
        println("done")
    }
}

throw carries a message; the nearest try catches it and binds it to the catch variable; finally always runs.

docs.title: Why this release matters
docs.text: Each of these is a piece the Stenopos compiler will need when it's rewritten in Stenopos: hash maps for interners, lists of tokens and AST nodes, byte-level string scanning for the lexer. Alpha.6 is the language growing up enough to describe itself. Generics and traits are next.
